about: Anoria: 150 more cards from real history, found only in packs (merged into the game on 2026-11-11: see `merged`; nothing in the game loads this file): 100 Figures, 20 Relics and 30 Deeds. cards: one object per card, with the fields of cards.js (key, n, t, f, c, m, reg, era, y, k, arr, insp, from) and of text.js (cap, ll, tx, fact, say, art; links holds the card's LINKS sentences as 'source>key'). A Relic or a Deed has `fx`, the card already in the game whose effect, cost and rules text it takes, and `fit`, one line on why the history suits that effect. src is the reference page for the card's dates, fact and links. Wikipedia could not be opened from the session that wrote the cards, so each card was checked through web search, which quotes Wikipedia and other pages; src2 is a second page the search quoted in support. sure is true when the search confirmed the card's dates, its fact and every link sentence, and false when it did not return one of them; check says what was not returned, or what the sources disagree about. Picture briefs (art) were written from memory and get the usual audit before any art is made. threads: named lines to collect, shaped like THREADS in cards.js. threadAdds: new cards that belong in a line cards.js already has. existing: links the new cards could give to cards already in the game (each needs a line in FROM or insp, and its sentence in LINKS). needsEngine: a few Relics and Deeds that are not among the 150, because each needs an effect the engine does not have. dropped: the cards that left the first draft, each with its reason. heldForGuides: five of those, kept whole, because a Guide's picture for each is on the working branch. merge: what the merge has to do that is not copying. Check with: node scripts/anoria/check-set.js

links.@library>euclid: Ancient writers place Euclid in Alexandria under the first Ptolemy, the king who began its Library.

cards.tx: Scholar: you draw a card when he arrives.
cards.fact: His Elements builds the whole of geometry, step by step, from a handful of plain starting points. It was copied, printed and taught from for more than two thousand years.
cards.art: Euclid about 300 BC in a shaded colonnade at Alexandria, teaching the first proof of his Elements: a spare Greek man of about fifty with a short grey beard, in a plain wool cloak, seated on a stone bench with a papyrus roll held open between his two hands, reading the next step aloud and glancing over the top of the roll. On the paving at his feet a young pupil kneels, swinging a cord pegged at one end to draw the second of two crossing circles in chalk, the triangle between them already ruled. Two more pupils lean in. The bright harbour shows between the columns. Seen from the pupil's side, low, so that Euclid's face and the roll are right of centre, about a fifth of the way down the picture. Nobody knows his face, so he is an ordinary Greek scholar of his day: no long white beard, no metal compasses with a hinge, no bound books. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain, with only column and shadow there: a plate sits in each top corner of the card.

links.@library>eratosthenes: Eratosthenes was the chief librarian of the Library of Alexandria.
links.archimedes>eratosthenes: Archimedes addressed his book The Method to his friend Eratosthenes.

cards.cap: Cyrene and Alexandria, c. 276 to c. 194 BC
cards.tx: Scholar: you draw a card when he arrives.
cards.fact: He worked out the distance around the Earth from the length of a shadow in Alexandria at noon on midsummer's day, when the Sun stood straight overhead in a town far to the south. His answer was close to the true one.
cards.art: Eratosthenes at noon on midsummer's day about 240 BC, measuring the Earth from a courtyard in Alexandria: a Greek scholar of about thirty-five, clean-shaven, in a light linen tunic with a cloak over one arm, down on one knee beside a bronze sundial bowl set on a low pillar, a hollow half-sphere with an upright pin at its centre. He is marking the tip of the pin's short shadow on the inside of the bowl with a reed pen, squinting against the glare, and his other hand shades his eyes. A boy holds an inkpot and a wax tablet. The sun is almost straight overhead, so every shadow in the white courtyard is small and sharp. Seen from the far side of the bowl, his face right of centre, about a fifth of the way down the picture. Ptolemaic Alexandria: no telescope, no globe, no glass lenses. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain, with only bare sunlit wall there: a plate sits in each top corner of the card.

cards.tx: Inspiring: your other Figures here get +1 Might.
cards.fact: He and his school taught that illness has natural causes, and that a doctor should watch the patient closely and note what happens day by day. Many new doctors still take an oath that carries his name.
cards.art: Hippocrates on the island of Kos about 400 BC, examining a patient in the open air: an old man with a bald crown and a short white beard, as the ancient busts named for him show, in a plain cloak that leaves one shoulder bare, bending with his ear laid flat against the bare back of a fisherman who sits on a stool, listening to the man's breathing with his eyes shut and one hand raised for quiet. Two students stand by, one with a wax tablet and stylus ready, the other holding a bowl and a sponge. They are in the dappled shade of a huge plane tree in a small harbour town. Seen from the side, from the waist up, the old doctor's head right of centre, about a fifth of the way down the picture. Classical Greece: no serpent staff, no white coat, no surgery or blood. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain, with only leaves and sky there: a plate sits in each top corner of the card.

cards.tx: When you play a Relic, draw a card.
cards.fact: In 132 he showed the Han court a bronze urn ringed with eight dragons, each holding a ball above an open-mouthed toad. When the ground shook far away one ball dropped, and it is said to have marked an earthquake days before riders brought the news.
cards.art: Zhang Heng, court astronomer of the Han dynasty, about AD 138, at the moment his earthquake urn proves itself: a slender scholar of sixty with a thin grey beard, in a long dark robe with wide sleeves, a sash and the tall lacquered cap of a Han official, standing with one hand raised and his head turned sharply toward a great bronze vessel shaped like a wine jar, as tall as a man. Eight bronze dragon heads point down around its shoulder, each with a ball in its jaws, and eight bronze toads squat below with their mouths open. One ball is in mid-air, falling from a dragon into a toad. Two junior officials have dropped their bamboo slips and stare. A timber hall with red pillars. Seen from across the vessel, Zhang Heng's face right of centre, about a fifth of the way down the picture. Eastern Han China: writing on bamboo slips and silk, no paper books, no chairs. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain, with only dark roof beams there: a plate sits in each top corner of the card.

cards.tx: Scholar: you draw a card when he arrives.
cards.fact: An official of the Han court, he reported to the emperor in 105 a way of making paper from tree bark, hemp, old rags and worn-out fishing nets. Paper of a rougher kind was older, but his was cheap and good enough to write on, and it spread across China.
cards.art: Cai Lun, an official of the imperial workshops of Han China, in AD 105: a beardless man of about fifty, as a palace eunuch was, in a plain belted robe with the sleeves tied back, standing at a wooden vat of grey pulp and lifting out with both hands a square bamboo frame stretched with cloth, water streaming from it and a thin even sheet of wet paper lying on the cloth. He tilts it to the light to judge it. Behind him two workers, one old and one young, pound bark and rags in a stone mortar, and a single finished sheet hangs over a pole to dry. Seen from across the vat, from the waist up, his face right of centre, about a fifth of the way down the picture and the dripping frame at the centre. Eastern Han China: no printed pages, no bound books, no writing on the sheets. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain, with only wall there: a plate sits in each top corner of the card.
cards.check: His birth year is given as anything from 50 to 62, so the caption gives only his death.

cards.tx: Scholar: you draw a card when he arrives.
cards.fact: His book of 628 is the first we know that treats zero as a number like any other, with rules for adding, taking away and multiplying with it. It speaks of numbers below zero as debts, and numbers above it as fortunes.
cards.art: Brahmagupta at thirty, in AD 628, an astronomer of western India, timing the rising of the Moon from a flat stone roof at dusk: a lean man with his hair tied in a knot on top of his head and a short beard, bare to the waist with a cotton shawl over one shoulder and a wrapped lower cloth. He sits cross-legged, sighting along a straight staff set upright on the parapet toward a huge moon just clearing the horizon, one hand lifted to give the signal. Beside him a pupil watches a water clock, a small copper bowl with a hole in its base slowly sinking in a larger basin, and keeps the count with pebbles. A bundle of palm-leaf pages tied between two boards lies by his knee. Seen from close by on the roof, his face right of centre, about a fifth of the way down the picture. India of the seventh century: palm-leaf pages, no paper books, no telescope, no turban of later centuries. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain, with only darkening sky there: a plate sits in each top corner of the card.
cards.check: The search confirmed the rules for zero and negative numbers; the words debts and fortunes were not returned.

links.brahmagupta>alkhwarizmi: Al-Khwarizmi's star tables follow the Sindhind, an Arabic version of Indian astronomy that is thought to come from Brahmagupta's book, and his own book on Indian numerals taught readers of Arabic to reckon with zero.

cards.tx: Legacy of Brahmagupta. Your Deeds cost 1 less.
cards.fact: His book on solving equations, written in Baghdad about 820, gave algebra its name, from the Arabic word al-jabr in its title. The word algorithm comes from his own name.
cards.art: Al-Khwarizmi about AD 820, on a canal bank outside the round city of Baghdad, putting his new method to work: a scholar of about forty with a full dark beard, in a long plain robe and a neatly wound turban, standing on the raised earth bank with a small wooden writing board held against his chest, a reed pen in his other hand, looking up from his reckoning to call a figure to two surveyors below who are stretching a knotted measuring rope across a field between stakes. A farmer and his brother wait at the field's edge for the answer that will divide their inheritance. Date palms, the canal, and far behind the wall of the city. Seen from the bank, from the waist up, his face right of centre, about a fifth of the way down the picture. Abbasid Iraq: no chalkboard of modern symbols, no x and y, no Ottoman dress. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain, with only pale sky there: a plate sits in each top corner of the card.
cards.check: That the Sindhind comes from Brahmagupta's book is generally presumed, not proven; the link says so.

links.alkhwarizmi>fibonacci: Fibonacci learned the Indian numerals as a boy in North Africa, and his book draws on al-Khwarizmi and the Arab mathematicians who followed him.

cards.tx: Legacy of Al-Khwarizmi. On arrival, gain 1 Spark.
cards.fact: His book of 1202 showed the merchants of Europe how to reckon with the nine Indian figures and zero in place of Roman numerals. One of its puzzles, about a pair of breeding rabbits, gives the string of numbers that now bears his name.
cards.art: Leonardo of Pisa, called Fibonacci, about 1202, in a merchant's counting house in Pisa: a man of about thirty with dark hair cut straight across the brow and no beard, in a long belted tunic and a soft cap, standing at a sloping desk and writing a column of Indian numerals with a quill, quick and sure, while he holds up his left hand to stop an older merchant beside him who is still pushing counters about on a lined counting board. The older man stares at the finished sum. Sacks, a pair of scales and bolts of cloth fill the room, and through the open arch behind stands the cathedral's new bell tower, only three storeys built and already leaning. Seen from across the desk, from the waist up, Fibonacci's face right of centre, about a fifth of the way down the picture. Pisa about 1200: no printed books, no eyeglasses, the tower unfinished. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain, with only stone wall there: a plate sits in each top corner of the card.

links.press>gutenberg: Gutenberg built his press in Mainz about 1450 and printed his great Bible on it.
links.paper>gutenberg: Most copies of Gutenberg's Bible were printed on paper, which cost far less than calfskin.

cards.tx: When you play a Relic, draw a card.
cards.fact: A goldsmith by training, he worked out how to cast metal letters by the thousand, all alike, in a small mould held in the hand. About 180 copies of his Bible were printed, and nearly fifty of them still exist.
cards.art: Johannes Gutenberg about 1450 in his workshop at Mainz, casting type: a man in his fifties in a plain dark gown with the sleeves rolled and a leather apron, a close cap on his head, standing by a small brick furnace. In his left hand he holds a little two-part mould of wood and iron that he has just snapped open, and a single bright new metal letter is dropping from it into his right palm; he peers at it closely. A ladle rests in the pot of molten metal, and on the bench are rows of finished letters, a file and a punch. Deep in the room behind, out of focus, stands the wooden press. Firelight on his face and hands. Seen from the bench, from the waist up, his face right of centre, about a fifth of the way down the picture. No portrait of him from life exists, so the face is an ordinary craftsman's: no long forked beard, no fur hat. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain, with only dark beams there: a plate sits in each top corner of the card.

cards.tx: Voyager. On arrival, gain 1 Spark.
cards.fact: He was the first to sail the Northwest Passage, in a small fishing boat with six companions, and he spent two winters on the way learning from the Netsilik Inuit how to dress in furs and drive dogs. In 1911 he used what they taught him to lead the first party to reach the South Pole.
cards.art: Roald Amundsen on 15 December 1911, aged thirty-nine, at the South Pole, fixing the spot with a sextant as his own account tells: a tall, lean Norwegian with a long weathered face, a large hooked nose, a heavy fair moustache white with frost and pale eyes narrowed against the glare, in a hooded anorak and trousers of reindeer fur made in the Inuit way, with fur mittens hanging from a cord around his neck. He kneels on one knee in the snow and looks through a brass sextant held in his bare hands, aimed down at a small flat tray of mercury set on a box, in which the low Sun is reflected. One companion, older and shorter, in the same kind of furs with his hood down and a full dark beard, crouches beside him with an open pocket watch and a notebook. Behind them stand one loaded sledge, a pair of skis planted upright and three sledge dogs, each different, one asleep, one sitting, one watching the men; each dog is about knee high to a man. The snow plain is flat and empty to the horizon. Seen from the snow in front of him, from the knees up, his head right of centre, about a fifth of the way down the picture. Historically accurate for 1911: no ice axes or ropes, no motor sledge, no ponies, no flag in this picture, no row of men. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain, with only pale polar sky there: a plate sits in each top corner of the card.

Written from memory and not searched: the Gjøa with seven men in all, the two winters at Gjoa Haven (1903 to 1905) and the Pole on 14 December 1911 are standard. The observations with sextant and mercury tray are in his own book, The South Pole.

links.copernicus>kepler: Kepler's first book, printed in 1596, was a defence of Copernicus's Sun-centred system.

cards.tx: Legacy of Copernicus. Scholar.
cards.fact: Working for years through another astronomer's sightings of Mars, he found that the planets move in ovals, not circles, and travel faster when they are nearer the Sun. He also defended his own mother in court when she was accused of witchcraft, and she went free.
cards.art: Johannes Kepler in Prague about 1605, at the end of his long war with the planet Mars: a thin, slight man of thirty-three with a pointed dark beard, in a black doublet with a small white collar, bent very close over a huge sheet of paper, for his eyes were weak, drawing with a pen the long oval path of a planet with the Sun set to one side of its centre. His free hand presses flat a stack of pages filled edge to edge with columns of figures, and more discarded pages cover the floor. The candles have burned down and grey dawn shows at a small leaded window; a brass quadrant hangs on the wall. Seen from across the table, low, his face right of centre, about a fifth of the way down the picture. Prague in 1605: he has no telescope yet, no globe of the planets, no wig. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain, with only wall there: a plate sits in each top corner of the card.

cards.tx: Voyager: she can walk to any Place.
cards.fact: Living in Constantinople as the British ambassador's wife, she saw old women guard children against smallpox by scratching a little matter from a mild case into the skin. She had her own son treated in 1718, and back in London she pressed doubting doctors to try it.
cards.art: Lady Mary Wortley Montagu in Constantinople in March 1718, having her son protected against smallpox: an Englishwoman of twenty-eight with dark hair, her face lightly pitted by the smallpox she survived and her eyelashes gone, wearing the Turkish dress she adopted and was painted in, a long fitted coat of patterned silk over a fine shift and loose trousers, a small jewelled cap. She kneels on a carpet holding her five-year-old son firmly on her lap, his sleeve rolled to the shoulder, her eyes fixed on the work. An old Greek woman in a dark headscarf bends over the boy's arm with a needle in one hand and half a walnut shell in the other. A window shows domes and cypress trees. Seen from close, Lady Mary's face right of centre, about a fifth of the way down the picture. Ottoman Constantinople in 1718: no harem fantasy, no veils over faces, no doctor's instruments of a later age. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain, with only wall there: a plate sits in each top corner of the card.
cards.check: The year 1718 for her son's inoculation was not returned.

links.newton>duchatelet: Émilie du Châtelet put Newton's Principia into French, and hers is still the standard French translation.

cards.tx: Legacy of Isaac Newton. Scholar.
cards.fact: She translated Newton's great book from Latin into French and added pages of her own to explain its mathematics. She finished the work in 1749, only days before she died.
cards.art: Émilie du Châtelet in the summer of 1749, working through the night to finish her translation of Newton: a tall woman of forty-two with a long, lively face and dark hair loosely dressed and unpowdered, in a loose silk morning gown with the sleeves pushed back, seated at a table crowded with candles. A great Latin folio stands open on a reading stand before her; she writes fast on a sheet with her right hand while her left holds a pair of brass dividers stepped across a diagram of an orbit. Finished pages lie in a deep pile at her elbow, tied in bundles with ribbon, and a cold cup of coffee stands forgotten. A tall window is black with night. Seen from the side, so that she is in profile from the waist up against the black window, her head right of centre, about a fifth of the way down the picture. France in the 1740s: no towering wig, no court hoops, no chalkboard. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain, with only dark panelled wall there: a plate sits in each top corner of the card.

links.montagu>jenner: As a boy, Jenner was himself protected against smallpox by the method Lady Mary Wortley Montagu had brought to England.

cards.tx: Legacy of Lady Mary Wortley Montagu. Steadfast: he has +2 Might when he defends.
cards.fact: In 1796 he scratched matter from a milkmaid's cowpox sore into a boy's arm and showed that the boy could no longer catch smallpox. The word vaccine comes from vacca, the Latin for cow, and in 1980 smallpox became the first human disease to be wiped out everywhere.
cards.art: Edward Jenner in May 1796 in a Gloucestershire dairy, studying the hand of the milkmaid Sarah Nelmes: a country doctor about to turn forty-seven with a round, kindly face and his own brown hair tied back, in a blue coat, yellow waistcoat and riding boots, holding the young woman's right hand in both of his and turning it to the light from the door to look at the blisters of cowpox on her fingers. She stands in a cap and apron, patient and a little amused. Behind them a brown and white cow turns her head in the stall, and a milking stool and wooden pail stand in the straw. A leather pocket case lies open on a barrel. Seen from inside the shed, from the waist up, Jenner's face right of centre, about a fifth of the way down the picture. England in the 1790s: no syringe, no white coat, no powdered court wig. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain, with only dark timber there: a plate sits in each top corner of the card.

cards.tx: Voyager. Inspiring: your other Figures here get +1 Might.
cards.fact: For five years he explored South and Central America, measuring everything from the heat of the sea to the blue of the sky. In 1802 he climbed higher on the volcano Chimborazo than anyone on record had ever climbed.
cards.art: Alexander von Humboldt on 23 June 1802, high on the volcano Chimborazo in the Andes, at the crack in the ridge that stopped him: a slim man of thirty-two with windblown light brown hair, in an ordinary town coat, waistcoat and thin boots cut to pieces by the rock, his lips and gums bleeding from the thin air. He kneels on a knife-edge of black rock and snow, holding a long glass barometer upright in its case and reading it with fierce attention, while a companion steadies the foot of the instrument and a third man writes the figure with numb fingers. Cloud boils below them on both sides and the white dome of the summit hangs close above. Seen from just along the ridge, from the knees up, his face right of centre, about a fifth of the way down the picture. No ropes, ice axes or climbing clothes of later times, no fur. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain, with only cloud there: a plate sits in each top corner of the card.

cards.fact: She was twelve when she and her brother dug an ichthyosaur out of the sea cliffs near their home, and she went on to find the first complete plesiosaur. She sold fossils for a living, and the learned men who bought them seldom gave her the credit.
cards.art: Mary Anning in December 1823 on the shore below the dark cliffs of Lyme Regis, uncovering the first complete plesiosaur: a sturdy young woman of twenty-four with a weathered face, in a heavy wool cloak, a long plain dress with mud to the knees and a bonnet tied down with a scarf, kneeling on a ledge of grey shale just washed bare by a winter storm. With a small hammer and chisel she is freeing the long line of neck bones that runs across the ledge to a tiny skull, and she has stopped, hammer lifted, to look at how long the neck is. A basket of tools stands beside her and her small black and white dog sits watching. Grey sea, wet rock, a landslip of clay behind. Seen from the seaward side, her face right of centre, about a fifth of the way down the picture, the fossil running down to the lower left. England in the 1820s: no dinosaur shown alive, no magnifying lens, no trousers. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain, with only cliff and sky there: a plate sits in each top corner of the card.

links.rosetta>champollion: The Rosetta Stone, with its Greek text beside the Egyptian, gave Champollion the way in to reading hieroglyphs.

cards.tx: Scholar: you draw a card when he arrives.
cards.fact: As a schoolboy he taught himself one ancient language after another, among them Coptic, the last form of ancient Egyptian. In 1822 he worked out how to read hieroglyphs, which nobody had been able to read for some fourteen centuries.
cards.art: Jean-François Champollion at noon on 14 September 1822, in his attic study in Paris, at the instant he understands the hieroglyphs: a dark, curly-haired man of thirty-one with a full face, in shirtsleeves and an open waistcoat, half risen from his chair so suddenly that it is tipping over behind him. In one hand he grips a sheet of paper copied from a temple wall, on which a ring of picture signs is drawn in ink, a sun disc first among them; his other hand is flat on the table among dictionaries and sheets of the same signs set out in rows. His mouth is open in a shout. Sunlight from a small window falls across the papers. Seen from across the table, from the waist up, his face right of centre, about a fifth of the way down the picture. Paris in 1822: no pith helmet, no pyramids through the window, no mummy. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain, with only sloping attic ceiling there: a plate sits in each top corner of the card.

cards.tx: Inspiring: your other Figures here get +1 Might.
cards.fact: In a British army hospital in the Crimean War she fought for clean wards, fresh air and decent food, and far fewer soldiers died. She was also a gifted statistician, and drew a new kind of chart to show that dirt and disease were killing more men than battle.
cards.art: Florence Nightingale in the winter of 1854 on her night round of the army hospital at Scutari: a slender woman of thirty-four with a calm, firm face and brown hair parted in the middle under a small white cap, in a plain black wool dress with a white collar and a short dark cape. She carries the lamp she really used, a Turkish lantern of folded waxed cloth like a small concertina with a metal top and base and a candle inside, held low at her side so that its glow lights her face from below. She has stopped at a low bed in a long corridor and bends to lay two fingers on the wrist of a sleeping soldier. Two more beds can be made out beyond his, each with a different man in it, one of them awake and watching her, and the rest of the corridor is lost in the dark: no rows of beds or of repeated figures. Seen from the foot of the bed, from the waist up, her face right of centre, about a fifth of the way down the picture. No brass oil lamp with a spout, no nurse's apron with a red cross, no starched veil. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain, with only darkness there: a plate sits in each top corner of the card.

links.jenner>pasteur: Pasteur gave his own method the name vaccination, in honour of Jenner's work with cowpox.

cards.tx: Legacy of Edward Jenner. Steadfast: he has +2 Might when he defends.
cards.fact: He showed that germs spoil food and cause disease, and that gentle heat kills them, which is why milk is pasteurised. In 1885 his new vaccine saved a nine-year-old boy who had been badly bitten by a rabid dog.
cards.art: Louis Pasteur in July 1885 in his laboratory in Paris, on the day the boy Joseph Meister is first treated: a grey-bearded man of sixty-two with a grave, anxious face, in a dark coat and a small black skullcap, his left arm held a little stiffly at his side. He stands with his right hand resting on the shoulder of a nine-year-old boy in a short jacket, whose bandaged hands and leg show the dog bites, and he watches without blinking as a doctor in the background draws liquid into a small glass syringe. On the bench beside them stand glass flasks with long bent necks and a tall jar in which a strip of dried tissue hangs from a thread. Daylight from a high window. Seen from the bench, from the waist up, Pasteur's face right of centre, about a fifth of the way down the picture, the boy lower and to the left. France in the 1880s: no white coats, no microscope held to the eye, no electric light. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain, with only wall there: a plate sits in each top corner of the card.

links.verne>bly: Nellie Bly set out in 1889 to beat the eighty days of Jules Verne's novel, and stopped in France on the way to meet him.

cards.tx: Voyager. Swift: she can walk on the turn she arrives.
cards.fact: A newspaper reporter, she went around the world alone in 1889 and 1890 with one small bag, by steamer, train, rickshaw and donkey, in seventy-two days. Two years earlier she had pretended to be mad to get herself locked in an asylum for ten days, and wrote about the cruelty she found there.
cards.art: Nellie Bly in January 1890 on the last leg of her race around the world, crossing America by special train: a small, quick young woman of twenty-five with a fringe of dark hair, in the one dress she took, plain dark blue wool, under a long checked travelling coat, a peaked cloth cap on her head. She stands on the open rear platform of a railway carriage with one hand gripping the iron rail and the other holding up a small leather handbag, the only luggage she carried, laughing into the wind as the track streams away behind. On a prairie station platform slipping past, four people wave hats and handkerchiefs, each different: a stationmaster, a farmer and his wife, and a boy running alongside. Steam and snow. Seen from the trackside, from the knees up, her face right of centre, about a fifth of the way down the picture. America in 1890: no trunk, no parasol, no bustle, no hot-air balloon (there is none in the book or in her journey). Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain, with only steam and sky there: a plate sits in each top corner of the card.

links.faraday>tesla: Tesla's motors run on electromagnetic induction, the effect that Faraday discovered.

cards.tx: On arrival, the strongest enemy Figure here misses its next turn.
cards.fact: He designed the alternating-current motors and power system that still carry electricity to homes around the world. On the lecture stage he made glass lamps glow with no wire leading to them.
cards.art: Nikola Tesla about 1892, lecturing in a darkened hall: a very tall, very thin man of thirty-six with black hair parted in the middle and a neat moustache, in a black tailcoat and white tie, standing alone on the stage with his arms lifted and spread. In each bare hand he holds a long glass tube with no wire leading to it, and both tubes are glowing with a cold white light that is the only light in the picture, throwing his face and shirt front into sharp relief. Behind him, half seen, stand two tall metal sheets on insulated posts and a table of coils. Three listeners in the front row are dark shapes at the bottom edge, each different. Seen from the stalls, from the knees up, his face right of centre, about a fifth of the way down the picture. In his lectures of 1891 to 1893 he lit tubes both ways, held in his hands and hung between the sheets; this picture shows them in his hands. No lightning bolts leaping about the room, no tower, no goggles. Correct anatomy, two hands, each holding one tube. cards.art: Chief Joseph of the Nez Perce in the late summer of 1877, leading the families of his people over a mountain pass on their long retreat: a tall, heavy-shouldered man of thirty-seven with a broad, grave face, his hair swept up in a high roll above the forehead with a long braid hanging in front of each shoulder, shell earrings, a striped trade blanket wrapped around him over a cloth shirt, leggings and beaded moccasins. He walks on foot at the head of a file, leading a spotted horse on which a small girl sits in front of an old woman, and he is looking back over his shoulder at those who follow, each different: a young mother with a baby on her back, an old man leading a pack horse that drags lodge poles, and a boy on foot. cards.art: Menelik II, emperor of Ethiopia, at first light on 1 March 1896 above the valley of Adwa: a big, dark, bearded man of fifty-one with a broad pockmarked face, in the dress he wore on campaign, a black silk cape over white cotton robes and a wide-brimmed dark felt hat, standing on a rocky spur under a great red umbrella held by an attendant. He has a field glass lowered in one hand and with the other signals forward one small mountain gun that its crew of three is dragging into place. Beside him stand two of his generals, each different, in lion's-mane collars and embroidered capes with round hide shields, and one priest in white with a tall processional cross. Below, between strange steep towers of rock, there are only dust, mist and gun flashes in the valley, and a few tiny white-robed riflemen going down toward them. Seen from on the spur, from the knees up, his face right of centre, about a fifth of the way down the picture. Ethiopia in 1896: no spears only, no bare feet and loincloths, no European crown. cards.fact: In 1297 he and Andrew Moray beat a larger English army at Stirling by waiting until part of it had crossed a narrow wooden bridge and then cutting that part off. A letter the two of them sent a month later, telling the merchants of Lübeck that Scotland was open for trade again, still exists.
cards.art: William Wallace on the morning of 11 September 1297, on the wooded crag above Stirling, watching the English army begin to cross the bridge below: a big, rawboned Scot of about twenty-seven with a short brown beard and hair to the collar (nobody knows his face, so he is an ordinary man of his time and place), in a knee-length padded and quilted linen coat with a mail collar, a plain iron helmet with a brim hanging from his belt, wool hose and leather shoes, a long spear upright in his left hand and a small plain triangular shield slung on his back. He crouches at the edge of the trees with his right arm stretched back, palm down, holding his men where they are. Two spearmen wait behind him, each different, one grey-haired and one a boy. Far below, small, a narrow timber bridge crosses a looping river, and on it a thin file of riders, two abreast, is coming over toward the marshy meadow on this side; a castle stands on its rock in the distance. Seen from the slope in front of him, from the knees up, his head right of centre, about a fifth of the way down the picture. Scotland in 1297: no kilt or tartan, no blue face paint, no two-handed sword on his back, no plate armour. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain, with only leaves and pale sky there: a plate sits in each top corner of the card.
cards.check: Added at the merge in place of Yaa Asantewaa, who is already a card. Written from memory and not searched: Stirling Bridge on 11 September 1297 with Andrew Moray and the Lübeck letter of 11 October 1297 are standard. His birth year is a guess in every source. cards.art: Enheduanna, high priestess of the moon god at Ur, about 2270 BC, composing a hymn at night, dressed as the carved stone disc that bears her own name shows her: a woman of about thirty-five with a strong profile and long hair falling down her back from under a round cap with a rolled brim, in a long robe of tiered woollen flounces that leaves one shoulder bare. She sits on a low stool on the flat roof of the temple house under a thin crescent moon, a small cushion-shaped tablet of damp clay in her left palm and a cut reed in her right hand, pressed to the clay; her lips are parted as she tries the line aloud. A lamp of oil burns in a shell beside her, and a servant waits with a basket of fresh clay. Below lie the mud-brick city and the palm groves along the river. Seen from the roof beside her, from the waist up, her face right of centre, about a fifth of the way down the picture. Early Mesopotamia: no great stepped tower yet (that was built two centuries later), no winged bulls, no Egyptian dress. cards.art: Aeschylus in the spring of 472 BC, in the theatre under the Acropolis of Athens, rehearsing his play The Persians: a broad, weathered man of fifty-three with a bald crown, a full grey beard and the scarred forearms of an old soldier, in a plain cloak. He stands on the beaten earth of the dancing floor, lifting a painted linen mask with a tall crown, wide eyes and an open mouth, and settling it over the head of an actor who wears a long robe with sleeves in the Persian fashion; a second actor waits with his own mask in his hand. Behind them three men of the chorus in eastern dress, each different in age and build, practise a slow step, and a piper tunes a double pipe. The audience seats are plain wooden benches on the hillside. Seen from the dancing floor, from the waist up, the playwright's face right of centre, about a fifth of the way down the picture. Athens in 472 BC: no stone theatre, no raised stage, no comedy masks. cards.art: Li Bai about 744, drinking alone under the Moon, as in the best known of his poems: a man of forty-three with a free, handsome face, a thin beard and bright eyes, in the loose robe of a Tang gentleman with wide sleeves, a black gauze cap pushed back on his head and a straight sword at his belt. He stands among blossoming trees on a terrace on a mountainside, his head tilted back, raising a small wine cup high in his right hand toward the full moon as if inviting it to drink, and his left arm is flung out. The moonlight throws his long shadow across the white stones behind him, so that he, the Moon and the shadow make a party of three. A wine jar stands on a rock. Seen from below the terrace, from the knees up, his face right of centre, about a fifth of the way down the picture and the Moon high at the centre. links.murasaki>seishonagon: Murasaki Shikibu and Sei Shōnagon served rival empresses, and Murasaki wrote in her diary that Sei was dreadfully conceited.

cards.tx: Scholar: you draw a card when she arrives.
cards.fact: A lady at the Japanese court, she filled a notebook with lists of things that delighted or annoyed her, sharp stories about the people around her and what she saw from day to day. It is called The Pillow Book, and people have been reading it for a thousand years.
cards.art: Sei Shōnagon about the year 995, on a snowy morning in the empress's rooms in Kyoto, in the best-known scene of her Pillow Book: a quick-witted court lady of about thirty with a pale oval face and hair that falls to the floor, in many layers of silk robes whose coloured edges show at the neck and sleeves. The empress has asked what the snow looks like on a mountain in an old Chinese poem, and Sei, instead of answering, has gone to the outer wall and is rolling up a hanging blind of fine bamboo with both hands, so that the white garden outside suddenly floods the dim room with light. Behind her the young empress, half hidden by a curtain stand, laughs, and other ladies look up from a charcoal brazier. Seen from inside the room, Sei from the knees up, her face turned back toward us right of centre, about a fifth of the way down the picture. Heian Japan: no writing desk in this picture, no later kimono with a wide sash, no fan held open. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain, with only dark ceiling there: a plate sits in each top corner of the card.
cards.check: Some scholars think Sei had left court before Murasaki arrived; the link says only that they served rival empresses.

cards.fact: He spent some thirty years writing the Shahnameh, the Book of Kings, which tells the story of Persia from the creation of the world in about fifty thousand rhyming couplets. It is one of the longest poems ever written by one person, and it helped to keep the Persian language alive.
cards.art: Ferdowsi about the year 1010, aged seventy, in the orchard of his house at Tus in eastern Persia, setting down the last lines of the Book of Kings: an old country gentleman with a long white beard and a tired, satisfied face, in a long quilted robe with a sash and a white turban, sitting on a carpet under a mulberry tree with a board across his knees. He has just lifted his reed pen from the page and holds it in the air. All around him on the carpet, in an open chest and stacked in a niche of the garden wall, are tied bundles of written pages, the work of thirty years, hundreds of them. A boy pours water from a ewer; a single saddled horse waits at the gate. Composed like a Persian manuscript painting, with flat bright colour and a high horizon. Seen from the carpet, from the waist up, his face right of centre, about a fifth of the way down the picture. Persia about the year 1000: no printed books, no heroes or monsters in the sky. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain, with only leaves there: a plate sits in each top corner of the card.

cards.art: Rumi about 1250 in the goldsmiths' street of the market at Konya, in the story his followers told of how the turning dance began: a scholar of about forty-three with a brown beard and a rapt, lifted face, in a wide-sleeved robe and a large wound turban, who has stopped in the middle of the lane with his eyes closed, his right arm rising and his left arm falling, the skirts of his robe just beginning to swing out as he turns in time to the ringing of hammers. In the open-fronted shop beside him a goldbeater and two apprentices, an old man, a youth and a boy, seated at their anvils, have looked up but keep hammering, sheets of gold leaf shining on the bench. Two passers-by, each different, stop with baskets on their heads. Seen from down the lane, from the knees up, his face right of centre, about a fifth of the way down the picture. He wears a worn black doublet with a small plain collar. He sits at a rough table by the inn's open door, writing with his right hand and holding the paper still with his left, which lies stiff and half closed, crippled by an old wound. He has looked up from the page and out of the door, amused, to where a thin old farmer on a bony horse and a stout man on a donkey are passing along the road in the heat, with a row of white windmills turning on the ridge behind them. A jug, bread, his saddlebags. Seen from inside the dark room, from the waist up, his face right of centre, about a fifth of the way down the picture. Spain about 1600: no wide cartwheel ruff, no knight in full armour. She leans steeply in from the right toward a tall canvas whose back is to us, her right arm stretched up and across with a long brush at its tip, her left hand low and holding a palette and more brushes, her eyes on a point of the canvas we cannot see. Hard light from a high window falls on her forehead, forearm and bare neck against a plain brown wall. Seen from close beside the easel, from the waist up, her face right of centre, about a fifth of the way down the picture. Nothing of the painted picture is shown. cards.art: Matsuo Bashō in the summer of 1689, aged forty-five, shooting the rapids of the Mogami River in the far north of Japan, swollen with the early summer rains, as his travel diary tells: a slight, weathered man with a shaved head, in the black robe of a lay monk hitched up at the knees, straw sandals and a wide round hat of woven sedge tied under his chin. He kneels in the middle of a long, narrow flat-bottomed rice boat that is racing bow-down between green cliffs, one hand gripping the side and the other clamping his hat to his head, his mouth open in something between terror and delight. Behind him his companion clings to their bundles, and a boatman stands in the stern leaning his whole weight on a long pole. White water, a thread of waterfall down the cliff, rain. Seen from the bank just ahead of the boat, Bashō from the waist up, his face right of centre, about a fifth of the way down the picture. Edo Japan: no sword, no samurai topknot. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain, with only wet cliff and leaves there: a plate sits in each top corner of the card.

cards.art: Johann Sebastian Bach in the late autumn of 1705, aged twenty, on his long walk across Germany to hear the old organist of Lübeck: a sturdy, square-faced young man with strong dark brows and his own brown hair tied back, in a long travelling coat, muddy boots and a broad hat, a leather satchel of music across his back and a stout stick in his hand. He has come over the last rise of a flat, wet road at sunset and stopped dead: ahead, across the marshes, stand the brick walls of the city and, above them, the two tall green spires of the great church he has walked three weeks to reach. He stares at them, breathing hard, with the beginning of a grin. A carter going the other way looks back at him. Seen from the road in front of him, from the knees up, his face right of centre, about a fifth of the way down the picture, the city small in the lower left. She sits at a small round table with a sheet of paper before her, a quill in her right hand held just above the page, her left hand raised with one finger against her cheek, looking up and away as the next line comes to her. On the table are an inkstand, one candle and a small thick book lying open. The room is dark and bare behind her. He has just been handed it; his eyes are shut and his head is thrown back, and he is drawing an enormous breath. On the desk in front of him lies the heap of coins he has paid, forty pounds, and behind the desk his former owner, a Quaker merchant in a plain brown coat and broad hat, is still holding the pen. A ship's captain claps Equiano on the shoulder. Through the door, the harbour and a sloop at anchor. The door of the room, behind her, has begun to open with a creak, and without turning her head she is sliding a sheet of blotting paper over the page with her left hand, her eyes going sideways toward the door and the corner of her mouth lifting. A work basket, a teapot, a garden beyond the glass. Seen from across the little table, from the waist up, her face right of centre, about a fifth of the way down the picture. cards.art: Sequoyah in 1821, showing the leaders of the Cherokee Nation that his signs can carry speech, with the help of his young daughter Ayoka: a man of about fifty with a calm, deep-lined face, dressed as the portrait painted of him in 1828 shows him, in a blue coat over a white shirt, a red cloth wound around his head as a turban, a long-stemmed pipe in his hand, sitting on a bench with his lame leg stretched out. Three headmen, each different, in turbans, hunting coats and trade-cloth shirts, lean toward her, one with his hand over his mouth. A log council house, a low fire. cards.tx: Legacy of Hokusai.

cards.art: Hiroshige in 1832, aged thirty-five, sketching on the great road from Edo to Kyoto as a sudden summer storm breaks: a round-faced, mild-looking man with a shaved crown and a small topknot, in a travelling kimono tucked up at the knees with leggings and straw sandals, sitting on the bench of a roadside tea stall under its dripping thatched eave. A small sketchbook is open on his knee and his brush is moving fast, but his eyes are on the road, where two bearers with a covered litter and a man hunched under a paper umbrella are running bent double up a hill into slanting grey rain, while a grove of bamboo behind them bows in the wind in three fading bands of grey. The tea woman holds out a cup he has not noticed. Seen from the road, looking in under the eave, Hiroshige from the waist up, his face right of centre, about a fifth of the way down the picture. Edo Japan: no great wave, no Mount Fuji, no samurai armour. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain, with only thatch and rain there: a plate sits in each top corner of the card.

links.shakespeare>goethe: Goethe wrote that the first page of Shakespeare he read made him Shakespeare's for life.

cards.tx: Legacy of Shakespeare. Scholar.
cards.fact: Poet, playwright, minister of a small German state and student of plants and colours, he worked on his great play Faust, about a scholar who bargains with the devil, for some sixty years. He finished it only months before he died.
cards.art: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe in April 1787, aged thirty-seven, in the public garden at Palermo in Sicily, where the idea came to him that all plants are variations on one plan: a tall, handsome man with large dark eyes, a strong nose and his brown hair tied back unpowdered, in a pale travelling coat, with a broad-brimmed grey hat lying on the path beside him. He has gone down on one knee in front of a bed of strange southern plants and holds a single large leaf flat on his palm, tracing its ribs with a pencil, while a pocket volume of Homer, which he came out to read, lies forgotten face down in the grass. Lemon trees, palms and tall flowering stems surround him, and the sea is blue beyond a wall.
