cards.fact: Born Erik Weisz in Budapest, he could slip out of handcuffs, chains, jail cells and a locked tank of water in which he hung upside down. He also spent years exposing fake mediums who claimed to speak with the dead.
cards.art: Harry Houdini about 1916, aged forty-two, hanging head down in a straitjacket high above a city street: a short, very muscular man with curly dark hair standing out from his head and a face clenched with effort, his ankles bound in a padded harness to a rope that runs up to a beam jutting from the top of a tall newspaper building. He is strapped into a canvas straitjacket with leather buckles, his arms crossed and pinned, and he is doubled up at the waist, twisting, with one shoulder already worked half free. He fills the upper part of the picture, upside down, and far beneath him the street is a soft blur of straw hats and stopped trams, with no faces drawn. At one near window four people lean out to watch, each different: a clerk in shirtsleeves, a woman with her hand to her mouth, a newsboy and an old man. Seen from a window level with him, his whole figure in the upper half, hanging right of centre, his face turned toward us enough to read (he hangs head down, so his feet, not his head, are nearest the top). He is drawn from the photographs and films of these escapes, respectfully and recognisably, with nothing invented. No chains, no water tank, no top hat or wand. Correct anatomy. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain, with only sky and the edge of the building there: a plate sits in each top corner of the card.

cards.tx: Voyager: he can walk to any Place.
cards.fact: A Sherpa who herded yaks as a boy in sight of Mount Everest, he first went to the mountain as a young porter in 1935 and went back six more times. In 1952 he climbed higher on it than anyone had before, and the year after that he stood on the top.
cards.art: Tenzing Norgay on 30 May 1953, aged thirty-nine, at the camp in the high valley below Mount Everest, the day after he stood on its summit, as the photographs taken that day show him: a lean, strong Sherpa with a wide, brilliant smile, deep creases at the corners of his eyes, a sun-darkened face with paler skin where his goggles sat, and thick black hair blown about, in a quilted down jacket open at the neck over a wool jersey, with a knotted scarf. He sits on a wooden ration box holding an enamel mug of tea in both bare hands, laughing at someone out of the picture. His ice axe is stuck upright in the snow beside him and his goggles hang at his chest. Behind him are one small orange tent, a coil of rope, and a wall of blue-white ice and snow rising out of the picture. He is the only person shown. Seen from close in front, from the waist up, his head right of centre, about a fifth of the way down the picture. He died within living memory, so this is a respectful, recognisable portrait taken from the photographs of him in 1953, at this documented moment, with nothing invented. 1953 clothing and gear: no modern bright climbing suit, no helmet, no flags in this picture, no oxygen mask on his face. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain, with only snow slope and deep blue sky there: a plate sits in each top corner of the card.
cards.check: Added at the merge in place of Amelia Earhart, who is already a card. Written from memory and not searched: seven expeditions to Everest between 1935 and 1953 and the height record of 1952 with Raymond Lambert are standard. His birth date is not certain (he took 29 May 1914), and he was born either in Khumbu or in Tibet and brought up in Khumbu; the caption gives Khumbu as his home.

links.hypatia>astrolabe: Hypatia's father Theon wrote a book on the astrolabe that later writers built on, and one of her students thanked her for teaching him how to make one.

cards.cap: Alexandria and Baghdad, from the 4th century
cards.tx: Your Figures can walk two steps.
cards.fit: A traveller who can read the sky knows the way.
cards.fact: With one brass disc a traveller could tell the time by the Sun or a star, find the direction of Mecca and measure the height of a tower. An astronomer of the tenth century described about a thousand uses for an astrolabe.
cards.art: A brass astrolabe of the Islamic world, made in Baghdad in the tenth century, hanging by its ring from the thumb of a raised hand against a clear night sky, seen from the front, close and a little from below. It is a flat round brass disc about as wide as the hand that holds it is long and as thick as a finger, not a ball and not a cage of rings. At its top a small solid three-lobed bracket carries a shackle and a loose ring; the thumb passes through the ring, so the disc hangs plumb below the hand. The disc has a raised outer rim engraved with fine ticks. Inside the rim lies its front plate, flat cut-out openwork: a narrow ring near the edge and, inside it, a second, smaller ring set off-centre, pushed up so that it touches the outer ring at the top and leaves a wide gap at the bottom. From the two rings sprout about fifteen short pointed tongues shaped like little flames or dagger blades, each one marking a star: they are of different sizes, scattered unevenly, a few inside the small ring and more in the wide gap below it, and they point in different directions, never evenly spaced round the edge like the hours of a clock. Through the gaps in the openwork one sees the solid plate beneath, engraved with a nest of fine circles that grow smaller toward a point above the centre, crossed by fanning arcs. One pin goes through the exact centre, held by a small wedge. It is lit warmly from below by a lamp that is out of the picture. Behind it, out of focus, are the flat roofs and one dome of a city and a field of stars. Only the hand and wrist of the holder are in the picture, in a plain wide sleeve, coming in from the right edge. Historically accurate: it must not look like a clock or a sundial: no clock hands, no straight bar or pointer arm across the front, no ring of evenly spaced marks, no lantern or lamp anywhere in the picture, no glass, no magnetic needle, no wheel spokes, no numbers or letters that can be read. The hand is small and high in the picture, right of centre, the wrist coming in from the right edge about a sixth of the way down; the instrument hangs just below it, in the middle of the picture, its centre about four tenths of the way down and its lower edge above the middle of the picture's lower half. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain dark sky.
cards.check: The search corrected the first draft: Theon's book was not the earliest on the astrolabe.

links.cailun>paper: Cai Lun showed the Han court in 105 how to make good paper from bark, hemp, rags and old nets.

cards.tx: Draw one more card each turn.
cards.fit: Cheap pages meant more books for more readers.
cards.fact: For centuries only China knew how to make paper. It reached Samarkand in the 700s and Baghdad before the year 800, and Spain about two hundred years after that, and wherever it arrived, books became cheaper.
cards.art: Newly made sheets of paper drying in the sun in a Chinese papermaker's yard of about the second century, in the Han dynasty, seen from low in the yard: a row of plain wooden frames, each about as wide as an arm is long and stretched with coarse woven cloth, leaning side by side against a long wall of pale rammed earth, and on every frame a pale, slightly rough sheet of paper drying on the cloth it was made on. The nearest sheet is dry: it has begun to lift from its cloth at one corner and curls away in the breeze, its fibres catching the light. In front of the wall stand a low wooden vat of grey pulp with one more cloth-covered frame resting across it, a stone mortar with a wooden pestle, and a basket of bark strips, rags and a tangle of old fishing net. A single finished sheet lies on a low table under a brush and an ink stone, still blank. No people. Historically accurate: the paper dries on its cloth frames, not pasted on the wall; no printed or written characters anywhere, no bound books, no scrolls on rollers, no glass. The drying frames fill the upper half of the picture. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain wall and sky.
cards.check: The search corrected the first draft: paper was in Muslim Spain by the 900s.

links.napoleon>rosetta: Soldiers of the army Napoleon took to Egypt found the Rosetta Stone in 1799, built into an old wall they were pulling down.

cards.tx: Draw one more card each turn.
cards.fit: One stone opened three thousand years of writing.
cards.fact: The same decree is carved on the stone three times: in hieroglyphs, in the everyday script of Egypt and in Greek. Scholars could read the Greek, and that was their way in to the other two.
cards.art: The Rosetta Stone as it was found in July 1799, half dug out of the rubble of an old fort wall in the Nile delta: one thick slab of dark grey stone standing tilted in a trench of sand and broken brick. It is about two thirds as tall as a man, three quarters as wide as it is tall and as thick as a forearm. It is a broken piece of a taller stone: its top edge is jagged, the whole upper left corner gone in one long slanting break, the upper right corner gone in a shorter break, and the lower right corner broken off; its left side and its bottom edge are straight. Its flat polished face is covered from top to bottom with fine carved writing in three bands that are plainly different from each other: at the top the shortest band, a few rows of small picture signs, cut through by the breaks; in the middle a taller band of a flowing, slanting script; and at the bottom the tallest band, many close rows of small neat square letters. All the writing is far too fine to read and is drawn as texture only. A soldier's pick and a wooden measuring rod lean beside it, and one hand in a dusty blue cuff has just brushed the dust from the middle band. Hard sunlight rakes across the carving. No people but the one hand. Historically accurate: no writing that can be read, no gold, no painted colours on the stone, no pyramids behind. The stone stands in the upper half of the picture, a little right of centre, seen from low in the trench. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain sky and wall.

cards.tx: Your Figures can walk two steps.
cards.fit: Thirty miles in an hour, where a horse did thirty in a day.
cards.fact: At trials near Liverpool in 1829 a locomotive named Rocket ran at about thirty miles an hour, a speed no horse could keep up for long. Within twenty years Britain had laid some six thousand miles of railway.
cards.art: The locomotive Rocket at speed at the trials of October 1829, seen from low beside the track a little ahead of it, coming toward us and to the right: a small engine painted bright yellow with black bands. At its front end stands a very tall thin white chimney, twice as tall as the men who ride behind it, held by two thin stays. Behind the chimney lies a short yellow barrel of a boiler, and behind that a squarer firebox. On each side there is one big spoked driving wheel at the front, under the chimney end, as tall as a man's chest, and one small wheel at the back under the firebox, half that height. On each side a cylinder is fixed high on the back end of the boiler and slants down and forward at a steep angle, its rod turning a pin on the big front wheel. There is no cab: the driver and the fireman, two different men in dark coats, stand in the open on a small platform behind the firebox, one holding his hat on. Coupled behind them is a low four-wheeled wagon carrying a big water barrel on its side and a heap of fuel. The engine runs on a plain iron track on a low embankment, white steam streaming back flat from the chimney top. A marquee with two flags stands far back; nobody else is in the picture. The engine is not too large in the picture: from the top of its chimney to the rails it takes up less than half the picture's height. The chimney stands in the middle of the picture, its top a fifth of the way down from the top edge, and the rails under the wheels run a little above two thirds of the way down, with the grassy bank below them. Historically accurate: big wheels in front and small wheels behind, no cab roof, no cowcatcher, no headlamp, no bell, no coupling rods between wheels, no later streamlining. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain sky and steam.

cards.tx: Once a turn, jump one of your Figures to any Place. It is done for the turn.
cards.fit: A balloon lifted people over everything that stood in their way.
cards.fact: The first passengers in a hot-air balloon, sent up before the king of France in 1783, were a sheep, a duck and a rooster. Two months later two men flew across Paris for about twenty-five minutes, feeding a fire of straw beneath the paper-lined bag as they went.
cards.art: The hot-air balloon of the Montgolfier brothers on 21 November 1783, floating over the roofs of Paris with the first two people ever to fly, seen from the air a short way off at the height of its gallery: a huge bag of cloth lined with paper, shaped like an egg standing on its narrow end, not a ball: about thirteen times as tall as a man and only two thirds as wide as it is tall, its top a broad dome, widest a third of the way down, and from there narrowing in a long taper to a round open neck at the bottom. It is painted a deep blue-green and gold: signs of the zodiac round the top, lily flowers and golden suns round the middle, and swags of drapery round the lower part. The neck passes down through the middle of a ring-shaped wicker gallery, which is fixed round the neck like a collar, with a waist-high rail hung with cloth, and on it, on opposite sides of the neck to balance it, stand two tiny men in coats and hats, each different. Get their scale right: a man standing in the gallery is only one thirteenth as tall as the balloon above him, no taller than one of the painted suns, and the gallery rail comes to his waist. One of them is waving his hat and the other is pushing a forkful of straw through an opening in the neck toward an iron fire basket that hangs by chains in the middle of the opening. A thread of smoke trails away. Far below lie grey slate roofs, church towers and the river with its bridges, and on one near roof three people, each different, looking up. The balloon is small in the picture and far off: from its crown to the fire basket under its gallery it is only a third of the picture's height. Its crown is a seventh of the way down from the top edge and its gallery is well above the middle of the picture, with wide open sky all round it, and the city is spread out below in the lower half. Historically accurate: no gas burner, no basket hanging on ropes, no net over the bag, no modern bright stripes, no letters. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain clear sky.

cards.tx: Once a turn, jump one of your Figures to any Place. It is done for the turn.
cards.fit: An aeroplane lifts a person over everything that stands in the way.
cards.fact: On 17 December 1903 two bicycle makers from Ohio, Orville and Wilbur Wright, made the first flights in a powered aeroplane. The first lasted twelve seconds and covered less ground than the wingspan of a modern airliner.
cards.art: The Wright brothers' aeroplane on the morning of 17 December 1903 at the instant it first leaves the ground, seen from behind it and to its right, as in the photograph taken that morning: a frail machine of spruce and pale unpainted cloth, flying away from us toward the left, about knee-high above the far end of a single wooden rail laid on flat sand. It has two long straight wings one above the other, about seven times as wide as a man is tall, joined by a row of thin upright struts and crossed wires. Far out in front of the wings, at the far left, a pair of small flat surfaces one above the other is held on long curved wooden runners that also serve as its sledge skids. Behind the wings, nearest to us, stand two tall narrow upright rudders side by side. Between the wings and the rudders two big slender two-bladed wooden propellers face backward, one on each side of the middle, turned by long chains from a small engine that sits on the lower wing. One man lies flat on his stomach on the lower wing beside the engine, head forward, his hips in a cradle and one hand on a lever. The other brother, a lean clean-shaven man in a dark suit and a flat cap, has just let go of the right wing tip and stands caught in mid-stride at the right, watching. A low wooden bench, a small box, a shovel and a coil of wire lie on the sand near us. Cold grey light, wind off the sea, flat sand to a low horizon. The machine is in the upper half, a little left of centre; the standing man is right of centre, his head lower than the top wing and well clear of the top right corner. Historically accurate: no wheels, no seat, no enclosed body, no tail plane, no propeller at the front, no engine cover. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain blank winter sky.
cards.check: The flights were at Kill Devil Hills, four miles from Kitty Hawk.

links.arminius>teutoburg: Arminius led three Roman legions into the Teutoburg Forest in AD 9 and destroyed them there.

cards.tx: One of your Figures clashes with an enemy at its Place with +1 Might, even if it has already acted.
cards.fit: A whole army was struck from behind a wall when it could not form up.
cards.fact: In AD 9 three Roman legions were strung out along a narrow track between a wooded hill and a bog, in the rain, when Arminius's warriors struck from behind a wall of turf. Traces of that wall and thousands of lost Roman things have been dug up at Kalkriese in Germany.
cards.art: The ambush in the Teutoburg Forest in September of AD 9, seen from low on the track, looking along it: a narrow, muddy path between a steep wooded slope on the left and a reedy bog on the right, in heavy slanting rain. Along the foot of the slope runs a chest-high wall of stacked cut turf topped with a fence of woven branches, running away into the picture, and over it three Germanic warriors, each different in age and build, are coming down onto the path: bareheaded men in wool tunics, trousers and cloaks, one with his hair tied in a knot at the side of his head, with long narrow wooden shields and spears with short iron heads. Facing them on the path are three Roman soldiers, each different, caught out of order: one in a mail shirt and a plain rounded iron helmet still pulling the leather rain cover off his big curved shield, one dragging at a loaded baggage mule, one turning with his short sword half drawn. In the mud at the lower right lies a Roman cavalryman's face mask of silvered iron, fallen and staring up, rain beading on it. The rest of both armies is hidden by rain and trees. All six men are small in the picture and close together, in one band that lies between a sixth and a half of the way down from the top edge: the wall with the three warriors coming over it at the left and in the middle of that band, the three Romans and the mule at the right and in the middle of it, the warriors only a little higher than the Romans; no head is in a top corner or above that band. Above the band are dark trees and rain; the lower half of the picture is the churned mud of the track, the reeds, and the fallen mask. No horned or winged helmets, no close view of wounds, no rows or columns of repeated figures. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain dark wet branches.

links.caesar>testudo: In his own account of invading Britain, Caesar tells how the Seventh Legion locked shields into a tortoise to storm a stronghold in the woods.

cards.tx: Quick. One of your Figures gets +2 Might for one clash. On the other player's turn it plays itself when it would save your Figure, paid for with 1 Spark you kept.
cards.fit: Locked shields carried soldiers through what would have stopped them.
cards.fact: Testudo is Latin for tortoise. Roman soldiers locked their shields edge to edge in front, at the sides and over their heads, and walked up to an enemy wall under a rain of arrows and stones.
cards.art: A Roman tortoise of shields in 54 BC, seen from the top of the stockade it is attacking, looking down on it: a tight block of some thirty soldiers has become a single roof of long oval shields, overlapping like tiles, with a wall of shields along the front and down both sides, and only sandalled feet, the rims of a few plain bronze helmets and the tips of a few short swords showing at the edges. Stones and javelins thrown from above are bouncing off the shield roof, one stone in mid-air, and a clay pot has just smashed across it. The block moves steadily toward us up a ramp of piled earth and brushwood among the stumps of felled trees. In the near corner at the bottom, the sharpened tops of two or three stockade logs and one defender's bare forearm, which has just let go of a stone. Nobody else is in the picture: the formation is the subject, small enough to be seen whole. Every shield is the same: a long oval curved like a section of barrel, with a long wooden rib down its middle and a small metal boss, painted with one simple pattern. The formation is small in the picture and seen whole, with bare trampled ground all round it: from its back row to the sandalled feet under its front wall of shields it takes up only a third of the picture's height, and it lies between a sixth and a half of the way down from the top edge. The lower half of the picture is the brushwood ramp, the stumps and the tops of the stockade logs. The late Roman Republic: oval shields, mail shirts, plain bronze helmets; no rectangular shields, no segmented plate armour, no red horsehair crests in a row. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain trampled earth and forest edge.
cards.check: Caesar, Gallic War 5.9.

links.douglass>brownsbox: Frederick Douglass wished Henry Brown's escape in a box had been kept quiet, so that others could have got away by the same road.

cards.tx: A Figure costing 3 or less arrives from your hand at any Place.
cards.fit: Henry Brown arrived where nobody could stop him, shut inside a box.
cards.fact: In 1849 Henry Brown, enslaved in Virginia, had himself nailed into a wooden box about three feet long and sent by express to Philadelphia. He travelled twenty-seven hours by wagon, train and steamboat, part of the way upside down, and stepped out a free man.
cards.art: Henry Brown's box on its way north in March 1849, on the freight deck of a river steamboat: a plain crate of rough boards, three feet long, two feet wide and two and a half feet deep, nailed shut and bound round with five hoops of split hickory, lying on its side among trunks, barrels and canvas mail sacks. A paper label is pasted on it, and three very small holes are bored in one end. Two travellers have just tipped it over to make a seat and are sitting on it side by side, with no idea what is under them: a stout older man in a tall hat and a greatcoat, lighting a pipe, and a thin younger man in a cloth cap with a carpet bag between his feet, who turns to him to ask what might be inside. A lantern swings from a beam of the deck roof above them; beyond a rail the wide grey river slides past, with the boat's tall thin smokestack and the round cover of its paddle wheel. Seen from across the deck, from a little way off, so that the men and the crate are not large in the picture: from the top of the tall hat down to the bottom edge of the crate is less than half of the picture's height. The top of the tall hat is a sixth of the way down from the top edge, and the whole crate, with all five of its hoops, its label and its bottom edge, is above the middle of the picture, in plain view between and below the two men's knees; nothing stands in front of it. The lower half of the picture is bare deck planks in lantern light and shadow, with one coil of rope. The two men's heads are near the middle of the picture's width, well clear of the top corners. Historically accurate: no bars, no chains, no person shown inside, no lettering that can be read. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain dark timbers of the deck roof.
cards.check: That he travelled part of the way upside down was not returned.

links.darwin>beagle: Charles Darwin sailed as naturalist on HMS Beagle, and filled the ship with the rocks, bones and animals he collected.

cards.tx: Draw 2 cards.
cards.fit: Five years of collecting came home in one small ship.
cards.fact: HMS Beagle was a small survey ship, only about ninety feet long, sent to chart the coasts of South America. Her voyage was meant to take two years and lasted almost five.
cards.art: HMS Beagle in 1834, lying at anchor in a narrow channel at the far southern tip of South America, seen from low on the water off her side: a small, sturdy wooden ship about ninety feet long with three masts, the first two crossed by yards with their sails furled and the third, shortest mast at the stern carrying no square yards; a white band runs along her dark hull, a slim boat hangs at each side near the stern and a small one across the stern. She is dwarfed by what stands behind her: a wall of dark beech forest rising straight from the water, and above it a great mountain of ice and snow whose glacier comes down to the sea. One of the ship's boats is pulling for the shore with four men, each different, and a pile of boxes and nets. On her cramped deck, small but plain to see, are a collector's things: crates, a net hung to dry, large bones laid out. Cold clear light, seabirds, a whale's back in the channel. The ship is a little above the middle of the picture, her mastheads about a fifth of the way down from the top edge, with the mountain rising behind and above her; the water, the whale and the boat are in the lower half. Historically accurate: no steam funnel, no paddle wheels, no gun smoke, no flag with stars. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain cloud on the mountain.
cards.check: Not returned by the search. The ship's length (90 feet) and the two years planned are standard, written from memory. At the merge: not searched again; it is standard and is left as written.

cards.tx: Gain 3 Spark.
cards.fit: Gold was lying in a river for whoever came.
cards.fact: Gold was found at a sawmill in California in January 1848. Within two years about a hundred thousand people had come by wagon and by ship, from as far away as Chile, China and Australia.
cards.art: A miner's pan in a California river in 1849, seen very close from just above the water, looking up the stream: a wide, shallow pan of dark sheet iron with a flat bottom and sloping sides, wider than a dinner plate, held up tilted toward us in two wet, cracked hands, with water and pale gravel pouring off its lower lip, a crescent of black sand left inside it, and in the black sand a scatter of bright yellow flakes and one small nugget. The pan and the hands fill the middle of the picture in its upper half, and the gold is right of centre. Only the miner's hands, his rolled wet shirt sleeves and one knee are in the picture. Beyond the pan the river runs away up a canyon past a wooden rocker box on the bank, two canvas tents, one mule and pine trees, and three other diggers, small and far off, each different: a Chinese miner in a loose dark jacket and a wide woven hat, a Chilean in a poncho and a flat-brimmed hat, a sailor in a striped shirt. River stones and a pick in the shallows below. Hard mountain light. No faces close up. Historically accurate: no machinery, no hoses, no town, no blue denim. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain pines and sky.

cards.tx: Enemy Figures at one Place miss their next turn.
cards.fit: For a day the men on both sides would not fight.
cards.fact: On Christmas Eve of 1914, in the first winter of the First World War, soldiers in the trenches of both sides began singing carols across the lines. In many places they climbed out next day to shake hands, swap small gifts and bury their dead, and here and there kicked a football about.
cards.art: Christmas Day of 1914 between the trenches in Flanders: a flat field of frozen mud, white with hard frost under a pale low sun in a still clear sky, crossed by two low tangles of barbed wire on wooden stakes. Out in the middle are six soldiers, three British and three German and each one different, their rifles left behind. They are not standing in a line: they make three separate pairs, one pair near us at the left, one a few steps farther off in the middle, one nearer again at the right, turned different ways, and every pair is one British soldier with one German. The British are in muddy khaki-brown: one in a sheepskin jerkin and a knitted woollen balaclava, one in a long khaki greatcoat and a soft peaked cloth cap, one with a muffler wound round his neck and a battered soft cap. The Germans are in faded grey-green tunics and tall boots: two in small round brimless cloth caps with a coloured band, and one bareheaded, because he has lent his helmet. In the near left pair the Briton in the sheepskin and a German are shaking hands. In the middle pair the Briton in the greatcoat holds out a round tin of tobacco and a German holds out a handful of cigars. In the right pair the Briton with the muffler has put the German's spiked leather helmet, in its plain grey cloth cover, on his own head, and the bareheaded German beside him is laughing and holding the Briton's cap. Along the parapet of the farther trench, small and far off, stands a row of five tiny fir trees with lit candles. Nobody else is in the picture. Breath smokes in the cold. Seen from the lip of the nearer trench, the six men from head to foot in the middle of the picture, their heads between a quarter and a third of the way down. Historically accurate for December 1914: no steel helmets on anyone, no gas masks, no fighting, no bodies, no tanks, no flags. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain pale winter sky.
cards.check: Not returned by the search. Standard, written from memory. At the merge: not searched again; it is standard and is left as written.

links.eleanor>magnacarta: King John, who was made to put his seal to Magna Carta in 1215, was Eleanor of Aquitaine's youngest son.

cards.tx: Enemy Figures at one Place miss their next turn.
cards.fit: The king's men were stopped by the law.
cards.fact: In 1215 the barons of England forced King John to put his seal to a long list of promises, among them that no free man would be jailed except by the law of the land. Four copies written out that summer still exist.
cards.art: The sealing of Magna Carta in the meadow of Runnymede beside the Thames in June 1215, seen close across a trestle table from a little above: a single large sheet of cream parchment, wider than a man's shoulders, covered edge to edge with close lines of small brown writing far too fine to read, lies on a cloth. From the folded foot of the sheet hangs a plaited cord, and on that cord a clerk's two bare, ink-stained hands are closing the two round bronze halves of a seal press, each the size of a saucer, on a lump of soft dark green wax: the king's great seal is pressed by a clerk, and nobody signs anything. Over the table hangs the striped cloth edge of an open tent, which hides every person from the chest up, so that we see only bodies, belts and hands: at the left three barons, each different in build, in long mail shirts under plain cloth surcoats, their hands in mail mittens resting on the round pommels of straight cross-hilted swords that hang at their belts; at the right one bare hand heavy with rings, from a sleeve of rich embroidered cloth, gripping the table's edge; and between them a bishop's gloved hand with one large ring, raised flat to keep the peace. Grass underfoot, a tent pole, bright river light behind. No faces at all. Historically accurate: no pen or quill in any hand, no crown on the table, no plate armour, no writing that can be read. Composition: we look across the table from the clerk's side; the table top fills the upper half of the picture, the parchment's far edge a quarter of the way down and the seal press exactly half way down, a little right of centre; the lower half of the picture is only the hanging table cloth, the grass and the clerk's two sleeves coming up from the bottom edge. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain striped tent cloth.
cards.check: The sealing at Runnymede and the four copies were confirmed. The search did not return the wording of the clause or that John was Eleanor's youngest son; both are standard. At the merge: not searched again; it is standard and is left as written.

links.aeschylus>marathonmarch: Aeschylus fought in the Athenian line at Marathon, where his brother was killed.

cards.fit: Having won one battle, they got up and marched to the next.
cards.fact: After beating the Persians on the beach at Marathon in 490 BC, the Athenians saw the enemy fleet put to sea and make for their undefended city. They hurried the twenty-five miles home, and were waiting above the shore when the ships arrived.
cards.art: The Athenian army after the battle of Marathon in 490 BC, hurrying home to save its city, seen from the road ahead: four tired Greek foot soldiers coming toward us along a dusty coast road between pines, each different in age and build, bronze Corinthian helmets, the kind with two eye holes and a nose guard, pushed back on the tops of their heads so that their faces show, big round bronze-faced shields slung on their backs, one long spear each sloped on the shoulder with its point up, linen and bronze body armour over short tunics, bronze greaves on their shins, grey with dust and sweat and none of them stopping. The nearest, a bearded man of thirty-five with a bandaged forearm, drinks from a goatskin as he walks; behind him a grey-bearded man has his arm around a limping young man of twenty; and a fourth looks out to sea. On the bright water to the right, far off, level with them and going the same way, three dark war galleys race them along the coast, each drawn clearly and seen exactly side on, travelling from left to right: each long, low and narrow, with a row of many thin oars along its side, one square sail on one mast, at the right-hand end, the bow, a straight pointed bronze ram that juts forward low at the waterline like a beak, with no upward curl at that end at all; at the left-hand end, the stern, the hull sweeps up into one tall curved fan. So only one end of each ship curves upward, the stern at the left. They are ancient Mediterranean galleys, not Viking ships: no dragon heads, no curled prow, no shields along the sides. The sun is low. Greece in 490 BC: no lone runner collapsing, no capes, no letters on the shields, no stirrups or horses, no column of repeated figures behind them. The nearest man's head is right of centre, a fifth of the way down. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain sky and pine branches.
cards.check: Herodotus 6.116. The search corrected the first draft: some scholars put the march on the day after the battle.

links.beethoven>ninth: The Ode to Joy is the last movement of Beethoven's Ninth Symphony, first played in Vienna in 1824.

cards.tx: Make one of your Figures ready, so it can act again.
cards.fit: The audience would not let the evening end.
cards.fact: At the first performance of his Ninth Symphony in 1824, Beethoven stood beside the conductor beating time, too deaf to hear the orchestra or the cheering. One of the singers turned him around by the sleeve so that he could see the audience on its feet.
cards.art: The end of the first performance of Beethoven's Ninth Symphony, in the Kaerntnertor theatre in Vienna on 7 May 1824, seen from the front row of the audience looking up at the stage: in the middle of the stage, among the wooden music stands of the orchestra, stands Beethoven at fifty-three, short and stocky, with a broad pock-marked face, a heavy jaw, fierce brows and a mane of untidy grey hair, in a dark green tailcoat and a white neckcloth. He has been standing with his back to the hall, bent over his score, and has heard nothing; only now is he being turned round to face us. The young solo singer Caroline Unger, twenty, with dark ringlets, in a pale high-waisted gown, holds his left sleeve in one hand and points out at the hall with the other, and he looks out over his shoulder, astonished, his right hand still raised from beating time. Behind them a violinist and a cellist of the orchestra, each different, one old and one young, have lowered their bows and are watching him. In the near foreground, dark against the candle light of the stage and cut off by the bottom edge, three raised arms of the audience wave a white handkerchief, a hat and a pair of gloves. Dark red curtain at both sides. No piano, no laurel wreath, no conductor's baton in his hand, no view of the auditorium, no row of footlights, no rows of faces. Beethoven's head is just right of centre, a fifth of the way down. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain dark stage curtain.

links.thoreau>saltmarch: Gandhi printed parts of Thoreau's essay on civil disobedience in his own newspaper in 1907, twenty-three years before he walked to the sea.

cards.tx: You count 4 more Might at a Place where you have a Figure, until the end of the round.
cards.fit: By the time it reached the sea, a walk of 79 people had become a crowd two miles long.
cards.fact: The march began with Gandhi and 78 companions and took 24 days. By the time they reached the sea the line of walkers was about two miles long, and within the year some sixty thousand people had gone to jail for making or selling salt.
cards.art: The shore at Dandi in western India on the morning of 6 April 1930, seen very close and low: an old man's thin, sinewy brown hand and forearm reaching down to lift a small lump of grey mud crusted white with natural salt from the wet sand at the edge of the sea. The arm comes from a short white homespun wrap; a tall bamboo staff is planted in the sand beside it, and a pair of worn leather sandals lies there. Behind, small and out of focus, stand only three companions in white homespun, each different: a tall old man with a long white beard and a white cap, a young man in a white cap, and a woman in a plain homespun sari with her hands pressed together; beyond them flat mud, small waves and pale early light. No face in close view, no soldiers, no police, no flags, no rows or columns of repeated figures. The hand and the lump of salt are right of centre in the upper half. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain morning sky.

links.douglass>emancipation: Frederick Douglass went to the White House in 1863 and again in 1864 to speak to Lincoln for the Black soldiers the Proclamation had brought into the army.

cards.tx: You count 4 more Might at a Place where you have a Figure, until the end of the round.
cards.fit: The Proclamation brought nearly two hundred thousand new soldiers to one side.
cards.fact: From 1 January 1863 the Proclamation declared free the people held as slaves in the states at war with the Union, and opened the army and navy to Black men. Nearly two hundred thousand of them served before the war ended.
cards.art: Watch Night, 31 December 1862, in a small plank praise house on the Union-held Sea Islands of South Carolina, a few minutes before the midnight on which the Emancipation Proclamation takes effect, seen from the middle of the room: an old Black man with white hair and a short white beard stands holding up a large silver pocket watch by its chain in the light of a single pine torch, its plain white dial marked only with ticks, and four people are gathered close around him, each different: a boy of ten with one hand raised, counting on his fingers; a mother in a headwrap lifting a baby to see; a woman praying with her eyes shut and her hands clasped; and at the open door a young Black man in the plain dark blue coat and cap of a Union soldier, a recruit of the first Black regiment camped nearby. Everyone else in the room is lost in darkness. On the plank wall hangs a sheet of printed paper, its print only fine grey lines. All the light comes from the torch, gold on their faces. Dignified, hopeful, tense. No chains, no whips, no overseer, no flags, no writing that can be read, no rows of repeated figures. The old man's head is right of centre, a fifth of the way down. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain dark rafters.
cards.check: The search did not return Douglass's night at Tremont Temple, so the link now gives his two visits to Lincoln.

cards.tx: Your Figures can walk two steps.
cards.fit: A rider with a foot braced on each side can stay in the saddle all day and go farther.
cards.fact: The oldest pair of stirrups that can be dated lay in the tomb of a nobleman buried in the north of China in 415. With a foot braced on each side a rider could stay in the saddle all day and stand up in it to fight.
cards.art: One of the earliest stirrups, from north China about the year 415, seen very close and large from the side as it hangs against the flank of a standing horse. It is one piece: a loop shaped like a triangle with rounded corners, a little wider than a foot, and a long flat straight handle rising from the top of the loop, nearly as long as the loop is high, with a slot near its top. The loop is the same narrow width all the way round, with no broad foot plate. It is made of bent wood covered in thin gilded bronze held by small rivets, and it hangs by a plain leather strap that passes through the slot in the handle and up to a wooden saddle with a high upright bow in front and another behind. A rider's soft leather boot rests in the loop, the ball of the foot on its lower bar; only the rider's leg below the knee is in the picture, in a loose trouser tied below the knee. The horse is a short, stocky steppe horse standing side-on and facing right. The picture shows the middle and front of the horse only: its shoulder, its chest and its two front legs at the right of the picture, the girth strap round its belly, and the rider's leg hanging just behind the front legs, where a rider really sits. The horse's hindquarters, hind legs and tail are outside the picture, beyond the left edge: no tail anywhere in the picture. There is no other person anywhere in the picture and no second stirrup: nothing hangs under the horse's belly. Beyond the horse, dry grass and low hills far away, evening light on the gilding. Historically accurate: no spurs, no horseshoes, no steel buckles, no armour on the horse. The stirrup is a little right of centre in the upper half of the picture. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain: sky, or the plain dark flank of the horse.
cards.check: The pair from the tomb of Feng Sufu (415) was confirmed as the earliest that can be dated; a tomb figure of 322 near Nanjing already shows a pair.

links.astrolabe>sextant: Before the sextant, sailors found how far north or south they were by measuring the height of the Sun with a seagoing astrolabe.

cards.tx: Once a turn, jump one of your Figures to any Place. It is done for the turn.
cards.fit: A ship that knows where it is can sail straight for its mark.
cards.fact: A sextant measures how high the Sun or a star stands above the horizon, and from that a navigator can work out how far north or south the ship is. Its curved scale is one sixth of a circle, which gave it its name. The first one was made in London in 1757.
cards.art: A brass sextant of about 1760 held up to the eye of a navigator on the deck of a sailing ship, seen close from his left side, so that he faces toward the left of the picture and we see the face of the instrument. It is a flat open frame of brass bars shaped like a narrow slice of pie, one sixth of a circle, about as long as a forearm from its point at the top to the curved edge at the bottom, held upright. Along the curved bottom edge runs a scale marked in fine lines. A flat brass arm is pivoted at the point at the top and swings down across the frame to the scale, where it ends in a small plate with a clamp screw. On the pivot at the top, fixed to the arm, stands one small upright rectangular mirror. Half way down the front edge of the frame, the edge farthest from his face, stands a second small upright glass, half of it mirror and half clear. On the edge nearest his face a short thin brass telescope is fixed across the frame, pointing level through that second glass toward the horizon; his right eye is at it. Two or three small dark glass shades on hinges sit between the two mirrors. His right hand grips a wooden handle on the far side of the frame, behind it, and the thumb and forefinger of his left hand hold the clamp at the foot of the swinging arm, sliding it along the scale. Only the two hands, the cuffs of a dark blue coat and, at the right edge, part of a cheek and the brim of a hat are in the picture. Beyond the instrument, to the left, are a ship's rail, a taut rope and the hard line of the sea's horizon, which the telescope is aimed at; the Sun is high, out of the picture, and glints on the top mirror. Historically accurate: two mirrors and one telescope, no compass dial, no numbers that can be read, no plastic, no drum with a handle on the arm. The sextant is in the middle of the upper half of the picture. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain sky.
cards.check: John Hadley's octant of 1731 came first; Captain John Campbell had it widened to a sixth of a circle in 1757, and John Bird made that first sextant. The link to the seagoing astrolabe is standard and was not searched. At the merge: not searched again; it is standard and is left as written.

cards.tx: Your Figures can walk two steps.
cards.fit: Where one river ended the canoe was carried to the next, so a journey did not stop.
cards.fact: The peoples of the northern forests of America built canoes of birch bark, stitched with spruce root and sealed with gum over a light wooden frame. A small one weighs about fifty pounds, no more than a child of seven, so a traveller could paddle to the end of one river and carry the canoe to the next.
cards.art: A birchbark canoe of the Ojibwe, about 1600, being carried over a portage trail between two lakes, seen from the side and from low down: one man walks toward the right with the canoe upside down over him, its middle crossbar resting on his shoulders and his two hands holding its edges in front of him, so that the hull hides his head and shoulders and he is seen from the chest down. The canoe is seen in full profile and is long, low and slender: about fourteen feet long, two and a half times his height, but only knee-deep, eight times as long as it is deep, so that it reaches far out in front of him and far out behind him, with both ends sweeping up in a rounded curve. Its skin is smooth sheets of birch bark, like tan leather, not woven: a warm golden tan marked with short dark horizontal flecks, sewn in panels with neat stitches of split root, the seams sealed with lines of black gum; its edges are bound round and round with root, and thin wooden ribs show inside. A paddle is tied inside along the crossbars. He wears hide leggings, a breechcloth and soft moccasins. On the near side of the trail, beside the back half of the canoe, a woman of the same people follows with a hide pack on her back, carried by a strap across her forehead; she wears a plain hide dress and her hair in one braid. Birch and spruce trees, a rocky path, bright water ahead. Only these two people. Historically accurate: no feather headdress, no painted designs on the bark, no metal fittings, no canvas, no basket weave. The canoe runs almost level across the whole width of the picture, a third of the way down from the top, its two ends lower than the top corners; the two people are small enough for the whole canoe to be seen. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain sky and leaves.
cards.check: Spruce root and spruce gum were confirmed (the United States National Park Service at Grand Portage), and a weight of about fifty pounds for a Wabanaki canoe. The year is only a place on the timeline: these canoes are far older.

links.pachacuti>ropebridge: The Inca roads, with their hanging bridges, grew with the empire that Pachacuti began.

cards.tx: Your Figures can walk two steps.
cards.fit: A bridge across a gorge saved days of climbing down one side and up the other.
cards.fact: The Inca crossed the gorges of the Andes on hanging bridges made of twisted grass. One of them still hangs over the Apurímac River in Peru, about thirty yards from cliff to cliff: every June the people of four villages cut the old bridge down and weave a new one in three days.
cards.art: A hanging bridge of twisted grass rope across a deep, narrow river gorge in the high Andes, seen from one end looking along it. Four cables as thick as a man's thigh, each plaited from three ropes of twisted grass, lie side by side to form the floor, which is covered with a mat of small sticks; two more cables at waist height form the handrails, and a web of thin cord laces each handrail to the floor, so that the bridge is a long open trough just wide enough for one person. The whole bridge sags in one long curve from footings of rough stone on this cliff to footings of rough stone on the far one, about thirty paces away. The rope is the colour of straw, fresh and bright. One woman in a full dark skirt, a woven shawl and a flat round hat is halfway across, small against the gorge, holding both rails; nobody else is on it. Far below, green river water; above, bare brown slopes. Historically accurate: no steel wire, no planks, no metal posts, no towers. The bridge runs from the lower left up to the right of centre, and the woman and the far end of the bridge are in the upper half of the picture. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain sky and rock.
cards.check: The yearly rebuilding in June by four Quechua communities, over three days, was confirmed; its length is given as 28 or 30 metres. That the road system grew under Pachacuti and his heirs is standard and was not returned. At the merge: not searched again; it is standard and is left as written.

cards.tx: Your Figures can walk two steps.
cards.fit: A load that rolls goes much farther in a day than a load that is carried.
cards.fact: The oldest wooden wheel yet found was dug out of a marsh in Slovenia in 2002 with its axle beside it. It is about 5,200 years old and is made of two planks of ash. Its square hole shows that wheel and axle were wedged together and turned as one.
cards.art: The oldest wooden wheel known, as it was about 3150 BC, on a small two-wheeled cart standing at the edge of a lake village in central Europe, seen very close from the side and from almost ground level, so that the wheel stands large against the sky. The wheel is a solid flat disc of pale ash wood about two and a half feet across, as high as a man's thigh, and as thick as two fingers, with no spokes: it is made of only two broad planks, each one a single wide board cut as half the disc, standing side by side, so that the one join between them runs straight up and down through the centre of the disc; there is no other seam anywhere on the disc, only the fine wavy grain of the wood. The two planks are held together by four long dark wooden battens that run from side to side across both planks, at right angles to the join and crossing it, each sunk into its own groove so that it lies level with the face of the wheel, with no nails, pegs or studs in it, and reaching almost from rim to rim: Count the battens: there are exactly four. Two are in the upper half of the disc and two are in the lower half, evenly spaced, all four parallel, like four dark level stripes across the pale disc. No batten touches or crosses the square hole: the middle band of the disc, where the hole is, is bare pale wood. At the exact centre is a square hole, and the square end of a round oak axle sits in it, sticking out by no more than a hand's breadth and jammed tight with small wooden wedges, so that the wheel and the axle turn together. The cart above is a plain narrow wooden frame of lashed poles and boards, with a single pole in front whose end rests on the ground. Mud and reeds underfoot; behind, a house standing on wooden posts over the water. No people and no animals. Historically accurate: no spokes, no metal rim, no nails, no round hub, not a disc of many narrow boards. The wheel fills the middle of the picture in the upper half. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain sky.
cards.check: Found in 2002; the age is given as 5,100 to 5,350 years. Ash wheel, oak axle, square hole and wedges were confirmed.

cards.tx: Draw one more card each turn.
cards.fit: Every count in the empire could be read off the cords.
cards.fact: The Inca kept the counts of a whole empire, its people, its llamas and its stores of maize, on knotted cords instead of in writing. The kind of knot and its place on the cord gave the ones, tens, hundreds and thousands. Herders in the Andes still keep count of their animals this way.
cards.art: An Inca quipu of about 1450 held up and spread out by two hands, seen close from the front: one thick main cord held between the hands in a shallow curve, and from it some forty thin cords of spun cotton hanging straight down side by side like a fringe, each one looped over the main cord at its top. The hanging cords are dyed in plain colours, cream, brown, dark green, gold and black, and each has clusters of small knots tied at three or four different heights, so that the knots line up in rough rows across the fringe; the lowest knots are long ones, wound several times. A few of the hanging cords have a shorter cord tied to them part way down. Only the two hands, the wrists and the edge of a tunic woven with small squares are in the picture; the hands are at the left and right edges about a quarter of the way down. Behind, out of focus, a wall of close-fitted grey stone and a row of storehouses on a hillside. Historically accurate: no beads, no feathers, no tassels, no writing. The fringe of cords hangs in the middle of the upper half of the picture. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain stone wall and sky.
cards.check: The place-value knots and the herders who still use them were confirmed. Several hundred quipus survive; nobody has an exact count.

links.@silk>starchart: The chart was found in 1907 in a sealed cave at Dunhuang, an oasis town on the Silk Road.

cards.tx: Draw one more card each turn.
cards.fit: A map of the whole sky, to be read a little further every night.
cards.fact: This paper scroll from Tang dynasty China is the oldest complete map of the night sky known from anywhere. It shows more than 1,300 stars in ink, group by group, and it lay with some forty thousand other manuscripts in a sealed cave until 1907.
cards.art: A Chinese star chart of about the year 670, a long narrow scroll of fine thin yellowed paper, only as wide as a hand is long, partly unrolled on a low wooden table and seen close from above at a steep slant, so that the table top fills most of the picture. Across the scroll run groups of stars drawn as small dots and circles in black and in red, joined into angular figures by thin straight ink lines, with a short column of small brush marks beside each group; at the unrolled end, in the upper half of the picture, is a round map of the stars about the pole, and among them, drawn a little larger than the rest so that it stands out, one group of exactly seven stars joined by one line in the shape of a ladle: four stars at the corners of a rough square for the bowl, and then a handle of three more stars, one after another in a bent line leading away from one corner of the bowl, so that the ladle has seven stars in all, never six. One hand in a wide grey sleeve holds the roll open while the other points with a thin bamboo stick at the ladle. A pot of brushes and an ink stone stand at the table's edge, lit by a lamp out of the picture; in the wall behind is a doorway onto desert cliffs under a night sky. No face. Historically accurate: stars joined by lines only, no pictures of animals or people among the stars, no writing that can be read, no telescope, no globe, no glass lamp chimney. The scroll runs from the lower left to the upper right of centre and the round map is right of centre in the upper half. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain dark wall and night sky.
cards.check: A study of 2009 counts 1,339 stars and dates it 649 to 684; an older estimate was about 940.

links.galileo>telescope: Galileo heard in 1609 of a Dutch spyglass, built better ones himself, and turned them on the sky.

cards.tx: Draw one more card each turn.
cards.fit: Every clear night the telescope showed something nobody had seen before.
cards.fact: Galileo's telescope was a tube with a glass lens at each end that made things look twenty times closer. In January 1610 he watched four small lights beside Jupiter change places from night to night, and understood that they were moons circling another world.
cards.art: Galileo's telescope of 1609 on a plain wooden stand at an open window in Padua on a January night, seen close from the side and from low down: one straight slender tube about as long as a walking stick and no thicker than a wrist, made of wood covered in dark red-brown leather with bands of fine gold tooling, with a short thicker collar at each end where a small lens sits. It rests in the fork of a simple wooden stand and points up at the sky through the window. On the windowsill beside it lies an open notebook with a column of small ink drawings, each one a small circle with three or four dots in a straight line beside it, in different places each time, and a quill in an inkpot. Outside, over tiled roofs and the domes of one church, a single bright planet stands in a clear dark sky. No people. Historically accurate: a plain straight tube with no eyepiece at the side, no mirror, no metal tripod, no brass draw tubes, no finder; nothing written that can be read. The tube runs from the lower left up to the right of centre, and its upper end is about a fifth of the way down from the top edge, clear of the top right corner. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain night sky and window frame.
cards.check: Britannica: he heard of the Dutch instrument in spring 1609, was observing at twenty times by the autumn and found the four moons in January 1610. Other accounts give his best telescope thirty times.

links.@timbuktu>manuscripts: The books were written and copied in Timbuktu, and families there have kept them from parent to child ever since.

cards.tx: Draw one more card each turn.
cards.fit: A city's learning, kept and copied in its own houses.
cards.fact: Families in Timbuktu have handed down handwritten books for hundreds of years, most of them in Arabic. When armed men seized the city in 2012, its librarians packed some 350,000 of them into ordinary metal trunks and sent them south to safety by road and by canoe on the Niger.
cards.art: A manuscript of Timbuktu lying open on top of others in a tin trunk, seen close from above at a slant: a book of loose leaves of thick cream paper, not sewn, kept in a worn wrapper of red-brown tooled leather with a pointed flap and a thong, its two open pages covered with neat close lines of brown and black handwriting, with notes written slantwise in the margins and one diagram of nested circles in red. The trunk is an ordinary painted metal one with a hasp, its lid thrown back, half full of other books stacked flat in their leather wrappers. A pair of hands in the wide sleeves of a pale blue robe is lowering one more wrapped book in at the side. A mud-brick wall behind, a strip of hard sunlight across the floor, a little sand. No face. Historically accurate: no writing that can be read, no printed pages, no gold, no bound spines. The open book is in the upper half of the picture, a little right of centre. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain mud wall.
cards.check: The trunks, the roads and the canoes on the Niger were confirmed. Counts of what was moved run from about 278,000 to 400,000. What the books are about was not returned, so the fact does not list it.

cards.tx: Draw one more card each turn.
cards.fit: News that took days by horse arrived in a moment.
cards.fact: On 24 May 1844 Samuel Morse tapped out a message in dots and dashes at the Capitol in Washington, and it was read in Baltimore at the same moment. By 1861 a wire ran across the United States, and five years later another lay under the Atlantic.
cards.art: The first telegraph of 1844 on a plain wooden table, seen close from the side and from table height. At the right a hand presses the sending key: a short springy brass lever on a small wooden base, with a round knob that one forefinger is pushing down. Beside it stands the receiving machine, as big as a mantel clock: an open brass frame of clockwork wheels, two fat upright coils of wound wire side by side, and above them a light brass lever that pecks a moving strip of paper against a small steel roller. The narrow paper tape comes off a large reel, runs through the machine and curls out across the table marked with a single row of short and long dents. At the back of the table stands a row of small glass tumblers, each holding a grey metal cylinder, joined one to the next by strips. Two cloth-covered wires run from the machine up the wall and out through a window frame to a wooden pole that carries glass knobs. A candle in a brass candlestick lights the brass. Only the hand, a white cuff and a dark coat sleeve are in the picture. Historically accurate: no telephone, no light bulb, no lamp with a glass chimney, no dial, no typewriter keys, no letters or numbers that can be read. The machine, the key and the tape are in the upper half of the picture, the machine a little right of centre. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain wall.
cards.check: 24 May 1844, the line across the United States (October 1861) and the lasting Atlantic cable (July 1866) were confirmed.

cards.tx: Draw one more card each turn.
cards.fit: Books opened to readers who could not see them.
cards.fact: Louis Braille lost his sight as a small boy. At school in Paris he was shown a soldier's code of raised dots for reading in the dark, and by the age of fifteen he had cut it down to a cell of six dots that one fingertip can cover. Those six dots make 63 different signs.
cards.art: A page of braille being read by touch about 1830, seen very close from the side and a little above: a sheet of thick cream paper on a sloping wooden desk, covered with straight rows of small raised dots that catch the low light from a window, each dot throwing a tiny shadow. The dots stand in small separate groups with a gap between one group and the next; no group is more than two dots wide or three dots high. The tip of a boy's right forefinger rests lightly on the dots of one row, moving from left to right, the other fingers curled loosely on the page, and his left hand lies flat lower down the page to keep the place. Beside the page lie the tools that made it: a flat wooden board holding another sheet under a narrow brass bar pierced with two rows of small upright windows, and a short blunt awl with a round wooden handle. Only the two hands and the cuffs of a dark school uniform are in the picture. Historically accurate: no printed letters, no pen and ink on the page, no spectacles, no typewriter. The page and the reading finger are in the upper half of the picture, the finger a little right of centre. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain wall and window light.
cards.check: The soldier's code (Charles Barbier's night writing), the six dots at fifteen in 1824 and the 63 signs were confirmed. Most sources say he was hurt at three; one says four.

cards.tx: Draw one more card each turn.
cards.fit: Once a thing was pressed into clay it no longer had to be remembered.
cards.fact: The oldest writing we know is on small tablets of clay from the city of Uruk, in what is now Iraq. They are not stories or prayers but accounts: so much grain, so many sheep, so much beer for the workers. About six thousand of these earliest tablets have been found.
cards.art: One of the earliest written tablets, from Uruk about 3200 BC, held in the palm of a left hand and seen very close from the front: a small cushion of pale brown clay no bigger than the palm it lies in, with rounded edges and corners, its face divided into four or five boxes by scratched lines. In each box a few simple signs have been drawn in the wet clay with a point: a jar with a pointed base, an ear of barley, a head beside a bowl; and beside them rows of small round dents and short thumbnail-shaped dents for numbers. The right hand holds a cut reed like a pencil, its tip resting in the last box. Only the two hands and bare forearms are in the picture. Behind, out of focus, big clay jars stand against a mud-brick wall. Historically accurate: drawn pictures and round number dents, not the later wedge writing; no rows of triangles, nothing that reads as a modern letter or numeral; the tablet is plain clay, not stone. The tablet is in the upper half of the picture, a little right of centre. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain mud-brick wall.
cards.check: Sources date the first tablets between 3300 and 3000 BC. The six thousand tablets and the beer rations (a tablet in the British Museum) were confirmed.

cards.fit: A canoe like this carried whole families to islands thousands of miles away.
cards.fact: Polynesian voyagers crossed thousands of miles of open Pacific in canoes with two hulls, steering by the stars, the swells and the flight of birds. A canoe some sixty feet long could carry two dozen people with their pigs, dogs, chickens and young plants, enough to settle an island.
cards.art: A Polynesian voyaging canoe far out on the open Pacific about a thousand years ago, just after sunset, seen from the water astern and to one side: two long slender wooden hulls of equal size, side by side a little apart, joined by a platform of lashed poles that carries a small thatched shelter, and driven by two tall sails on two masts. Each sail is shaped like a crab's claw: a tall narrow triangle standing on its point, its two long edges held by curved wooden spars, its top edge a deep hollow curve between the two spar tips, made of pale plaited matting. The canoe is about ten times as long as a man is tall and rides up the face of a long ocean swell. At the stern the navigator stands braced at a long steering paddle, an older man in a wrapped bark-cloth garment, his face lifted to the first bright star low ahead. Three other people are aboard, each different: a woman tending young plants wrapped in leaves, a boy bailing, a man asleep against a basket; one pig and some gourds of water are beside them. Two white sea birds fly the same way overhead. Historically accurate: two equal hulls, not one hull with a float; no carved figurehead, no flower garlands, no compass, no cloth flags. The canoe is not large in the picture: from the tips of its sails down to the water under its two hulls it takes up less than half of the picture's height. The sail tips are a seventh of the way down from the top edge and the two hulls ride the crest of the swell just above the middle of the picture, both hulls plainly seen side by side with a gap of dark water between them; the lower half of the picture is the dark face of the swell. The sails are a little right of centre. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain darkening sky.
cards.check: Sizes differ: canoes of fifty to sixty feet for two dozen people (PBS), about twenty metres as a rule (Te Ara). When each island group was settled is still argued over, so the fact gives no dates.

cards.fit: A longship could cross a sea and then be rowed far up a river.
cards.fact: A longship was long, light and so shallow that it could be rowed up a river or run straight onto a beach. One built in Norway about 890, with places for 32 oars, was dug out of a burial mound almost whole in 1880, and in 1893 a copy of it crossed the Atlantic in about four weeks.
cards.art: A Viking ship of about 890, the one found at Gokstad in Norway, under sail on a grey northern sea, seen from the water off her right side, a little ahead of her and from low down, far enough away for the whole ship to be seen: she sails toward the right, so that her right side faces us, her bow at the right of the picture and her stern at the left. She is a very long, low, slender open ship, not a small boat: fourteen times as long as a man is tall and nearly five times as long as she is wide. Get the scale of the men right: the ship reaches almost from one side of the picture to the other, and a man standing on her is no taller than one fourteenth of her length, so the men are tiny figures, a seated man's head only just above the row of shields, and the steersman much shorter than the stern post beside him. The mast is about half as tall as the ship is long. She is built of overlapping oak planks, each plank's lower edge lapping over the one below, sixteen planks high, sharp at both ends, with a plain curved stem rising high at the bow and at the stern, ending in a simple point. She has one mast amidships with one great square sail of wool in broad upright stripes, hung from a single yard. Along the whole length of the rail on this side hangs a long row of thirty-two small round shields, each one half covering the next, alternately black and yellow; a shield is only as wide as a man's arm is long. On this near side, close to the stern at the left of the picture, a big steering oar like the blade of a great oar is fixed to the hull and reaches down into the water; one man stands there holding the short bar at its top. Seven other men, each different in age and build, bareheaded or in plain caps, sit low along her length or haul on a rope: four aft of the mast, one beside it and two in the bow. Spray, gulls, a line of mountains far off. Historically accurate: no horned helmets, no dragon head, no rudder on the sternpost, no cabin or deck house, no second mast, no oars out while she sails. The ship reaches almost from one side of the picture to the other, a little above the middle; the sail is in the upper half of the picture, in the middle, the top of the mast a sixth of the way down from the top edge, and both stem tips are well below the top corners. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain cloudy sky.
cards.check: Built about 890, 32 oars, about 24 metres long and dug up in 1880: confirmed. The copy named Viking crossed in 1893 in 22 or 27 days, depending on the source.
