cards.fit: Robert Smalls took a whole ship's company out from under the guns to the other side.
cards.fact: Before dawn on 13 May 1862 Robert Smalls, the enslaved pilot of a Confederate steamer in Charleston, put on the captain's straw hat, picked up his own family and the families of his crew, and steamed out past the harbour forts, giving the right signal at each. He handed the ship to the Union fleet.
cards.art: The Confederate steamer Planter slipping out of Charleston harbour past Fort Sumter at about a quarter past four in the morning of 13 May 1862, seen from the water off her bow: a low wooden side-wheel steamboat, her hull close to the water, with one big rounded paddle box on each side amidships, a long low deckhouse, one tall thin black funnel standing just behind a small square wheelhouse perched on top at the front, and a short cannon on her foredeck, moving quietly through grey water in the half-dark before dawn. At the open window of the wheelhouse one man leans out with his arms folded across his chest, the way her captain always stood: Robert Smalls, a young Black man of twenty-three, in the captain's dark coat and the captain's huge wide-brimmed straw hat pulled low over his face. A small white plume of steam rises from the whistle beside the funnel: he is giving the signal. No one else can be seen on deck. Behind and above the ship rise the dark brick walls of Fort Sumter, a five-sided fort three rows of gun ports high standing straight out of the water, whole and unbroken, with one lantern and one small sentry on the parapet. Historically accurate: no white flag yet and no flag in view at all from this angle, no gun smoke, no sails, no people in chains. The wheelhouse and the man are right of centre in the upper half. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain dark sky.
cards.check: The captain's hat, the signals at Fort Sumter at about 4.15 to 4.30 in the morning and the families taken aboard were confirmed. How many people were on the ship was not returned, so the fact gives no number.

links.champollion>hieroglyphs: On 27 September 1822 Champollion's letter was read out in Paris, showing how the hieroglyphs spell names by their sounds.
links.rosetta>hieroglyphs: The Greek on the Rosetta Stone told scholars what the Egyptian beside it had to say.

cards.tx: Draw 2 cards.
cards.fit: A dead script could suddenly be read, and with it everything written in it.
cards.fact: In the ancient writing of Egypt the names of kings and queens are ringed with an oval. Champollion matched the signs inside two of those ovals, Ptolemy and Cleopatra, with the same names in Greek, and so had the sounds of a dozen signs. With them he went on to read names that no Greek had written down.
cards.art: A scholar's desk in an attic room in Paris in September 1822, seen close from above at a slant: a large sheet of paper on which two long ovals with a bar across one end, the rings the Egyptians drew around royal names, have been copied in ink one above the other. The two ovals hold two different names, so their rows of small picture signs are different. The upper oval holds seven signs, from left to right: a small square, a half-circle, a looped cord, a lion lying down, a small trough shape, two reed leaves side by side, and a hook. The lower oval holds nine signs, from left to right: a small triangle, a lion lying down, one reed leaf, a looped cord, a small square, an eagle standing in profile, an open hand, a mouth shaped like a lens, and a second eagle. Only three signs are in both ovals, the lion, the square and the looped cord, and three thin pencil lines slant across the paper to join each of them to its twin. The scholar's right hand, coming in from the lower right, holds a pencil with its point on the lower lion; his left hand, coming in from the lower left, pins down a printed engraving of a tall slim stone obelisk on a base. Around the sheet lie a candle burned low in a brass stick, a stack of worn books, an inkwell with a quill standing in it, and a cup. Only the two hands and their frayed shirt cuffs are in the picture; no face. Grey morning light from a small window. Historically accurate: true Egyptian hieroglyphs inside two ovals, no pyramids, no mummy, no sphinx, no writing in modern letters anywhere. The sheet with the two ovals is right of centre in the upper half. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain wall and window.
cards.check: The letter (read on 27 September, signed on the 22nd) and the twelve signs won from the ovals of Ptolemy and Cleopatra were confirmed; so was his reading of the name Ramesses from Abu Simbel on 14 September.

links.newton>halley: Edmond Halley used Newton's law of gravity to show that the comets of 1531, 1607 and 1682 were one comet coming back.

cards.tx: Make one of your Figures ready, so it can act again.
cards.fit: The comet came back when Halley had said it would.
cards.fact: Edmond Halley worked out that one comet had been seen three times, about 76 years apart, and said it would be back around 1758. He died in 1742. On Christmas night of 1758 a farmer near Dresden who watched the sky as a hobby found it with his own telescope, the first return of a comet ever foretold.
cards.art: Christmas night of 1758 on a farm at Prohlis near Dresden, seen from the snowy yard: a broad-shouldered Saxon farmer of thirty-five, clean-shaven, in a heavy wool coat, a knitted cap and boots, stands at the left with one eye to the small eyepiece at the lower end of a long slim telescope of dark wood and brass, longer than he is tall, which rests on a wooden trestle stand and slants up to the right, pointed low over the snow-covered roof of a timber-framed barn. In the clear black sky just above the barn roof, among sharp winter stars, hangs a small soft round patch of light, dimmer than the bright stars around it, with only the faintest short wisp of a tail: the comet. The telescope is aimed straight at the comet. A square tin candle lantern with thin horn panes and a ring on top, a candle burning inside it, stands in the snow at his feet beside an open notebook, and his breath smokes. Nobody else; one warm lit window in the low farmhouse behind. Historically accurate: the comet is small and dim, not a blazing streak; no observatory dome, no wig, no tricorne hat, and no glass paraffin lamp or hurricane lantern, which had not been invented. The farmer's head is left of centre, a third of the way down; the comet is right of centre, a fifth of the way down. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain black sky with a few stars.
cards.check: Johann Georg Palitzsch, farmer and amateur astronomer, 25 December 1758 (one source says Christmas Eve), and Halley's death in 1742 were confirmed.

links.magellan>naovictoria: The Victoria was the last of the five ships that Magellan led out of Spain in 1519.

cards.tx: Gain 3 Spark.
cards.fit: The Victoria's one cargo of cloves paid for the whole voyage.
cards.fact: On 6 September 1522 one small, leaking ship, the Victoria, reached Spain from the south with eighteen men on board, three years after sailing west. She was the first ship to go around the world. The cloves in her hold were worth more than the whole fleet of five ships had cost.
cards.art: The ship Victoria coming into the mouth of the Guadalquivir at Sanlucar in Spain on 6 September 1522, the first ship to sail around the world, seen from a small empty rowing boat close under her side: a short, round-bellied wooden carrack of the early 1500s, about seven times as long as a man is tall. She is built like a carrack: a raised forecastle at the bow, a low open waist amidships, and a raised half-deck and plain sterncastle at the stern; three masts, the foremast and the tall mainmast each with one big square sail and the mainmast with a round basket top, and on the small mast at the stern one three-cornered lateen sail. Her paint is gone, her sails are patched and grey, green weed hangs along her waterline, and a thin stream of water runs from a wooden pump over her side. At the rail of the waist, small against the ship, stand three of her crew, each different and all of them thin, bearded, barefoot and in ragged shirts: one shading his eyes toward the shore, one working the pump handle, one sitting slumped against the rail too weak to stand. In the near foreground, in the small boat, an open sack spills dark brown cloves, each like a small nail with a round head, across a plank; nobody is in the small boat. Low sandy shore, a small white town with one church tower, hard afternoon light. Historically accurate: no gun smoke, no crowd on the shore, no flags, no later galleon's high carved stern, no rows of gun ports, not a Viking ship or an open boat. The ship's hull and masts are right of centre in the upper half. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain sky.
cards.check: 6 September 1522 at Sanlúcar and the eighteen men were confirmed (some lists count seventeen Europeans and the men taken on in Asia). Sources say the cloves, about 26 tons, covered the cost of the expedition or were worth twice as much.

links.archimedes>syracuse: Archimedes designed the machines on the walls of Syracuse, his own city, when the Romans attacked it from the sea.

cards.tx: Quick. One of your Figures gets +2 Might for one clash. On the other player's turn it plays itself when it would save your Figure, paid for with 1 Spark you kept.
cards.fit: Archimedes's machines saved the wall at the moment the attack came.
cards.fact: When a Roman fleet came against Syracuse in 213 BC, the historian Polybius says, beams swung out over the walls and dropped great weights on the ships, and iron claws caught others by the bow and stood them on end. The city held out for more than a year.
cards.art: The sea wall of Syracuse in 213 BC in the first grey light after a night attack, seen from the water below and to one side: a high wall of pale stone blocks rising straight from the sea, and over its top a great wooden beam, as long as the wall is tall, swung out on a pivot like the arm of a crane. From the beam's end a heavy chain runs down to an iron grapple shaped like a hand with three hooked fingers, which has caught the bow of one Roman warship and is hauling it up out of the water, so that the ship stands steeply tilted on its stern with its oars hanging loose and water pouring off it. The ship is a galley: its bronze ram is at the bow, the high end, held in the claw; its curved sternpost and two steering oars are at the low end, still in the sea. Three Roman soldiers, each different, in bronze helmets with a knob on top and with long oval shields, cling to its rail. On the wall top, small, two Greek defenders steady the beam with ropes. A second ship is backing away at the lower left. Historically accurate, after Polybius: one ship lifted by its bow, no burning mirrors, no fire, no cannon, no rows of identical soldiers. The beam, the claw and the lifted bow are right of centre in the upper half. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain sky.
cards.check: Polybius (Histories 8.6) was confirmed for the weights and the claws; the siege ran from spring 213 to the autumn of 212. Whether a claw could lift a large warship is still argued about, so the fact gives it as his account.

cards.tx: Draw 2 cards.
cards.fit: A spoiled dish turned out to be a find.
cards.fact: In September 1928 Alexander Fleming came back from holiday to his laboratory in London and found that mould had got into one of his dishes of bacteria. Around the mould the bacteria had gone. The medicine made from that mould, penicillin, was ready for patients in the 1940s.
cards.art: A round glass culture dish held up to a window in a hospital laboratory in London in September 1928, seen very close: a shallow flat dish about as wide as a hand is long, its floor covered with a thin layer of clear amber jelly dotted all over with small round cream-gold spots, and near one edge a single large fluffy white patch of mould with a pale blue-green heart. All around that patch there is a clear ring where the spots have faded to ghosts and vanished; only farther away is the dish crowded with them. A thumb and two fingers hold the dish upright by its edge; a white coat cuff shows. Behind, out of focus, a crowded wooden bench of other glass dishes in stacks, a brass microscope, a rack of glass tubes plugged with cotton wool, a gas burner, and a sash window with brick chimney pots beyond. No face. Historically accurate: glass, not plastic; bare fingers, no rubber gloves, no printed labels, no writing. The dish is right of centre in the upper half. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain wall and window.
cards.check: 3 September 1928 and the dish were confirmed. Where he had been on holiday differs between sources, and one writer doubts the usual story because his first notebook entry is dated 30 October.

links.shakespeare>folio: Seven years after Shakespeare died, two actors of his own company gathered his plays into one book.
links.press>folio: About 750 copies were printed in London, and some 230 of them still exist.

cards.tx: Draw 2 cards.
cards.fit: About half his plays came down to us through this one book.
cards.fact: In 1623 John Heminges and Henry Condell, who had acted beside Shakespeare, had 36 of his plays printed in one large book. About half of them had never been printed before, among them Macbeth, Julius Caesar, Twelfth Night and The Tempest, and without the book they would probably be lost.
cards.art: A printer's workshop in London in 1623, seen close across a table: a tall stack of large printed sheets, folded once and gathered but not yet bound, the top sheet showing a page of two columns of small print inside ruled borders, the print only fine grey lines too small to read; and beside the stack one finished copy bound in plain brown calfskin, as tall as a forearm, lying shut. Two men stand behind the table, and a row of freshly printed sheets, each folded over a wooden rail near the ceiling like washing over a bar, with no pegs or clips, each showing two columns of fine grey print, crosses the top of the picture and hides both of them from the shoulders up, so that we see hands and clothes and no faces: one older man in an actor's good black doublet with white cuffs, laying a bundle of worn handwritten playbooks tied with string on the table; the other a printer in a leather apron black with ink, his sleeves rolled, lifting a fresh damp sheet by its two top corners. Behind them the heavy wooden frame and screw of a hand printing press with its long pull bar, and two round leather ink balls on a shelf. Candle and window light. Historically accurate: no writing that can be read, no portrait on any page, no quill being used, no modern machinery. Composition: the table top is in the upper half of the picture, the top of the stack of sheets a third of the way down and right of centre, the bound book beside it; the lower half is only the front of the heavy table and the floor. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain hanging paper and dark beams.
cards.check: Heminges and Condell, the 36 plays, about 750 copies and 230 to 235 survivors were confirmed. That eighteen of the plays were first printed here is standard and was not returned, so the fact says about half. At the merge: not searched again; it is standard and is left as written.

links.michelangelo>david: Michelangelo was twenty-nine when his David was unveiled in Florence.

cards.tx: You count 4 more Might at a Place where you have a Figure, until the end of the round.
cards.fit: A giant came to stand at the city's door.
cards.fact: Michelangelo's David is seventeen feet tall, about three times the height of a man. It took forty men four days to move it the half mile from his workshop to the main square of Florence, hanging upright in a wooden cage that rolled on greased beams. It was unveiled there on 8 September 1504.
cards.art: The moving of Michelangelo's David through a street of Florence in May 1504, seen close from the street, from among the workmen and a little below. The picture shows the colossal white marble statue only from the waist up: its chest, shoulders, arms and head rise above the front of a tall cage of heavy timbers, and everything of the statue below the waist is out of sight behind the cage's close-set front: broad horizontal beams, crossed diagonal braces and thick lashings of rope. Thick ropes run up from under the statue's arms to a beam across the top of the cage, because the statue hangs in the cage and does not stand. The statue is Michelangelo's David as it is known: the right arm hanging straight at its side, the left arm bent with the hand raised to the left shoulder holding a sling, the head with thick curls turned sharply to its own left, frowning. The statue is about three times the height of the men, so its head is far above them. In front of the cage, three workmen, each different in age, build and dress, in caps, shirts and hose of 1504: one leans his whole weight on a long wooden lever, one carries a short beam on his shoulder, one kneels and pours grease from a clay pot onto a wooden beam lying on the paving stones under the cage. A narrow street of plain stone houses; at its far end, small, the battlemented stone tower of the Palazzo della Signoria, where the statue is going. Morning light on the marble. Historically accurate: the statue is whole and unbroken, no pedestal, no rows of identical workers. The top of the cage is below the top edge of the picture, with sky above it; the statue's head is a little right of centre, a fifth of the way down the picture, well clear of the top edge. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain sky between the roofs.
cards.check: The height (5.17 metres), the forty men, four days, the cage on greased beams and 8 September 1504 were confirmed. Sources give the arrival in the square as 18 May or 8 June.

cards.tx: Enemy Figures at one Place miss their next turn.
cards.fit: The uproar in the hall stopped everything else.
cards.fact: At the first night of Stravinsky's ballet The Rite of Spring, in Paris on 29 May 1913, people in the audience shouted, whistled and argued so loudly that the dancers could not hear the orchestra. Most accounts say the man who had made the dance, Nijinsky, called the counts to them from the side of the stage.
cards.art: The wings of the stage at the Theatre des Champs-Elysees in Paris on 29 May 1913, the first night of The Rite of Spring, seen from deep in the wings looking across the stage, side on: in the near shadow, among hanging ropes and the wooden back of a canvas flat, a slight young man of twenty-four with slanting eyes, high cheekbones and dark hair, in a black evening tailcoat and white shirt front, stands on a plain wooden chair, leaning forward, one hand gripping a rope, the other beating the air, his mouth wide open, shouting the counts to the dancers; from the left edge two hands in dark sleeves hold him back by the tails of his coat. Beyond him, out in the hard stage light, three dancers, each different, are caught in the middle of a heavy, flat-footed jump with their knees bent and their feet turned in: two young women with long braids and headbands and one man in a pointed cap with a false beard, all in long loose cream smocks painted with bands of red patterns at the hem, cuffs and neck, belted, with soft boots bound with cross-straps up the shin. Behind the dancers is the painted backcloth of the ballet: green hills, grey boulders and a great streaked sky. The audience and the front of the stage are out of sight; nothing of the hall is in the picture. Historically accurate: no tutus, no pointe shoes, no tights, no footlights, no rows of identical dancers. The standing man's head is right of centre, a fifth of the way down. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain dark curtain.
cards.check: The date, the theatre and the noise were confirmed. Stravinsky said Nijinsky shouted the counts from a chair in the wings; the company's stage manager remembered him standing silent, so the fact says most accounts.

cards.tx: Make one of your Figures ready, so it can act again.
cards.fit: Shut out of the hall, Marian Anderson sang all the same.
cards.fact: In 1939 the great singer Marian Anderson was refused the biggest concert hall in Washington because she was Black. So on Easter Sunday she sang from the steps of the Lincoln Memorial instead, in the open air, to 75,000 people and to millions more by radio.
cards.art: Marian Anderson singing from the steps of the Lincoln Memorial in Washington on Easter Sunday, 9 April 1939, seen from the side and a little below: a tall, composed Black woman of forty-two with a calm oval face, her eyes closed, her head lifted a little and her mouth open in song, standing very straight with her hands clasped in front of her, in a long dark mink fur coat worn open at the throat over a bright scarf, and a small dark close-fitting hat. In front of her stands a cluster of six old-fashioned radio microphones on thin stands at the height of her chin. Behind her rise two of the great fluted white marble columns of the memorial, and between them, in deep shadow, the seated marble figure can just be made out. At the left edge a black grand piano with its lid raised and its player, an older white-haired man in a dark overcoat, seated on a bench. The listeners are not shown except as a soft band of colour far below at the bottom edge. Cold bright afternoon. Dignified and still. Historically accurate: no banner, no flags, no modern loudspeakers, no rows of faces. Her head is right of centre, a fifth of the way down. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain pale sky and stone.
cards.check: Easter Sunday 9 April 1939, the 75,000 and the refusal of Constitution Hall by the Daughters of the American Revolution were confirmed; the society itself said the hall was already booked that day. Her coat and the microphones in the picture brief are from the photographs and need a check against them.

cards.tx: Gain 3 Spark.
cards.fit: A franc a seat, and before long the seats were full all day.
cards.fact: On 28 December 1895, in a basement room of a café in Paris, the brothers Auguste and Louis Lumière showed ten films, each less than a minute long, to people who had paid one franc. Fewer than forty came that first evening.
cards.art: The first paid film show of the Lumiere brothers, in a low basement room under a cafe in Paris on 28 December 1895, seen from behind and to one side of the projector: in the near foreground, on a tall wooden stand, the Cinematographe, a polished walnut box no bigger than a hat box with a small crank handle on its side, turned by one hand that comes in from the left edge in a dark sleeve; a short brass lens sticks out of the far face of the box, pointing away from us at the screen, and from that lens a cone of light widens across the dark room to the screen. Close behind the box, nearer to us, stands a separate black metal lamp house with a little chimney, shining forward into the back of the box. On a white cloth screen at the far end is a grey, black-and-white picture of a factory gate with workers walking out toward us: women in long skirts, pale blouses and wide hats, and one man pushing a bicycle. Between the projector and the screen sit only four spectators on cane chairs, seen from behind, each different: a man in a top hat leaning forward, a woman in a feathered hat with her hand to her mouth, an old man with a cane, a young woman turning to her neighbour. Historically accurate: the picture on the screen is black and white and silent, no train rushing at the audience, no electric projector, no reels above the box, no lens facing us, no rows of identical heads. The screen is right of centre in the upper half. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain dark wall.
cards.check: The date, the Salon Indien of the Grand Café, the ten films and the one franc were confirmed; the audience is given as 33, 35 or about 40. A paid show in Berlin by the Skladanowsky brothers was eight weeks earlier, so the card does not call this the first.

cards.tx: Swap two Figures at different Places. At least one must be yours.
cards.fit: Two men changed places across a line.
cards.fact: On the morning of 10 February 1962 two prisoners walked past each other on a bridge at the edge of Berlin, between East and West: Francis Gary Powers, an American pilot shot down over the Soviet Union, and Rudolf Abel, a Soviet spy caught in New York. Each went home.
cards.art: The Glienicke Bridge between Potsdam and West Berlin on the cold grey morning of 10 February 1962, seen from the roadway near one end, looking along it: a long steel road bridge painted pale green, its two side girders riveted lattice trusses whose top edge sweeps up to a peak over each of two river piers and sags low between them, like the chains of a suspension bridge; the roadway empty and wet, with a white line painted across it at the middle. At the line two prisoners are passing each other, walking in opposite directions, a few steps apart, each alone: one tall and young in a heavy dark overcoat and a Russian fur hat, carrying a small case, walking toward us; the other thin, stooped and older, bald and hatless, with spectacles, in a dark overcoat, carrying a bundle, walking away. They do not look at each other. Well behind each of them, small, stand two officials in overcoats and hats. Bare winter trees on the banks, mist on the water. Historically accurate: morning, not night; no searchlights, no soldiers in rows, no barbed wire on the bridge, no flags. The two men are right of centre in the upper half, small against the bridge. Keep the top left corner and the top right corner plain grey sky.
cards.check: The date, the bridge, the two men and the morning hour were confirmed. A third man, the American student Frederic Pryor, was freed at Checkpoint Charlie as part of the same bargain.

links.caesar>rubicon: In January of 49 BC Caesar led the Thirteenth Legion across the Rubicon, the small river that marked the edge of Italy.

cards.tx: Jump one of your Figures to any Place. It is done for the turn.
cards.fit: Caesar was over the line and far down the road before anyone could stop him.
cards.fact: A Roman general had to give up his army before he came home to Italy. In January of 49 BC Julius Caesar crossed the little river Rubicon, the border, with a single legion at his back. From that step there was no going back, and it began a civil war.
cards.art: The river Rubicon at first light on a January morning in 49 BC, seen from the Italian bank, low at the water's edge: a stream so narrow and shallow that a man can wade it in ten strides, running between low banks of wet brown reeds. Three soldiers of the late Roman Republic are wading across toward us, each different in age and build, bare-legged, in mail shirts and plain bronze helmets with a small knob on top, with long oval shields slung on their backs: the first, a grey veteran, is already stepping out onto this bank with water streaming from his hobnailed sandal-boots; the second carries a pole topped with a silver eagle; and the third, a young recruit of eighteen, looks back over his shoulder at the bank they have left. On this side, in the mud at the lower left, are the fresh footprints of one man who has gone on ahead, already filling with water. A little upstream at the right, small, a plank footbridge on two trestles crosses the stream, with nobody on it. One torch burns on the far bank. Mist, a leafless willow, a few last stars in a paling sky. On the night before 1 March 1896 three Italian columns set out in the dark along separate mountain tracks to surprise them. The Ethiopians were waiting, and by the end of the day the invaders were beaten.
cards.art: The hills east of Adwa in Ethiopia at first light on 1 March 1896, seen from an Ethiopian position looking down a rocky slope: in the foreground three Ethiopians, each different, wait behind boulders: a grey-bearded nobleman wearing on his head a tall band of long tawny lion's-mane hair that stands up round his brow like a crown of fur (only the hair of the mane: no lion's face, no ears, no muzzle, no whole lion skin), and on his shoulders a cape of embroidered velvet edged with lion's mane over a white robe, with a long curved sword at his side and a round hide shield covered with silver bosses and filigree; a young rifleman in a white cotton wrap with a cartridge belt round his waist, aiming a single-shot breech-loading rifle with a wooden stock down the slope; and a woman in a white cotton dress bringing a water gourd. Down in the valley, small, a short broken line of soldiers in pale uniforms, some in tropical helmets and some in red caps, is coming out of the mist. cards.art: The top of Mount Everest at half past eleven on the morning of 29 May 1953, seen from a few steps below the summit: a small rounded cone of snow against a sky so dark it is almost black, and on it one man standing, Tenzing Norgay, in a bulky dark windproof smock and trousers with the hood up, big pale knee-high boots with metal spikes strapped under them, thick mittens, his face entirely hidden by an oxygen mask with a ribbed hose and by dark snow goggles, an open frame with one oxygen cylinder on his back, a rope tied round his waist. He holds his ice axe up in his right hand above his head, and a string of four small flags blows out sideways from its shaft. The rope runs from his waist down to the lower left corner, where the mittened hand of his partner comes into the picture holding a small folding camera. Below and behind them the white ridges of other great mountains fall away under a floor of cloud. Only these two people, and only one of them seen whole. cards.fact: About 1259 BC the kings of Egypt and of the Hittites swore to end their long war and never to attack each other again. cards.art: The peace treaty between Egypt and the Hittites as the Hittite king sent it to Egypt about 1259 BC, seen close over a table of dark wood: a flat tablet of bright silver about the size of a large book, covered with fine straight rows of tiny wedge-shaped marks pressed like bird tracks, and in the middle of it a round seal as wide as a palm, showing a tall god with a pointed cap embracing a smaller king. Two people hold the tablet upright between them from opposite sides of the table, and we see only their hands and forearms: from the left a brown Egyptian hand with a broad gold bracelet and a sleeve of fine pleated white linen; from the right a paler hand with a seal ring on one finger, in the long fringed woollen sleeve of a Hittite envoy. On the table below lie a clay tablet with the same wedge marks and a roll of papyrus. No faces. Sunlight through a doorway, one painted column with a lotus-bud top behind. Historically accurate: wedge-shaped cuneiform marks on the silver and no Egyptian picture signs on it, no weapons on the table, no coins, no writing that can be read. cards.art: The first look into Tutankhamun's tomb on 26 November 1922, seen from inside the dark room looking back at the blocked doorway: a wall of rough plastered stones with a small ragged hole broken through its upper corner, and through the hole a bare hand holding a lit candle and, behind it, part of a man's face peering in: one wide eye, a dark eyebrow, a neat dark moustache and a clean-shaven chin; bareheaded, no hat, no beard. The candle's flickering light falls into the room on three things only. First, standing against the wall in the lower left, one life-size wooden statue of a king standing guard, seen in profile and facing right: its skin is painted shining black, and it wears a gold headcloth, a broad gold collar, a stiff gold kilt and gold sandals, and holds a tall gold staff upright in one hand and a short gold mace in the other; it is the height of a man. cards.fact: In September 1940 Marcel Ravidat, who was eighteen, and three friends widened a hole left by a fallen tree near the village of Montignac in France and climbed down with a lamp. On the walls were horses, bulls and deer larger than life, painted by people who lived some 17,000 to 20,000 years before.
cards.art: The painted cave of Lascaux on 12 September 1940, seen from the floor looking up: a French country boy of eighteen in a patched jacket, shorts and heavy boots stands at the lower left with his back half to us, holding up a small home-made oil lamp, and its yellow light spreads over a curving wall and ceiling of pale chalky rock covered with animals painted in black, red and ochre exactly in the cave's own Stone Age style, flat and simple, not modern drawing: one great wild bull drawn only in thick black outline, with exactly two long horns curving forward and a muzzle marked with black dots, three times as long as the boy is tall, facing a line of four small horses painted the cave's way, with small heads, fat round bellies, short thin legs, stiff upright black manes like a brush and ochre flanks, no flowing manes or tails; above them one red cow with two short curved horns and no antlers; and between them two small red stags with branching antlers. A second boy, younger and smaller, is only a pair of legs sliding down a slope of loose stones from a dark opening at the left edge. Nobody else. Every new Relic and Deed here has `as`: the existing card whose effect, cost and rules text it takes. To play them, the engine (and the EV handlers in ui.js that name those keys) must look up `CARDS[key].as || key` where it now compares the key. Two Relics with the same `as` do the same thing, so a player should not be able to have both in play (hasRelic should compare `as`).
